results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
**How long you must keep tax‑related records**

| Record type | Recommended retention period | Source |
|-------------|------------------------------|--------|
| **All other tax records** (e.g., receipts, invoices, bank statements, payroll documents) that support items on a tax return | Until the **period of limitation** expires for the year the return was filed (i.e., the time the IRS can assess additional tax or you can amend a return) | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Copies of filed tax returns** (the return itself and accompanying schedules) | Keep a copy forever, because it helps prepare future returns and prove what was filed | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Employment‑tax records** (time‑keeping, payroll reports, federal employment‑tax statements such as Forms 941, 944, 940) | For **at least 4 years** after the date the employment tax becomes due or the tax becomes paid, whichever is later | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Records relating to property (assets)** that you use for business or capital gains purposes | Keep until the period of limitation has expired for the year you **dispose of (sell, trade, otherwise dispose of)** the property | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Other records no longer needed for tax purposes** | Do **not discard** until you confirm that they are no longer required for other legal or business purposes (e.g., insurance, creditor claims) | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Period‑of‑limitations table (general**

| Situation | Limitation period | Source |
|-----------|-------------------|--------|
| Owe additional tax, or claim a refund, or amend a return | **3 years** | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |
| Fail to report income that should have been reported and is >25 % of gross income | **6 years** | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |
| File a fraudulent return | **No time limit** | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |

**Special note on refunds**

If you file a refund claim, you must do so **within 3 years from the date you filed the original return or 2 years from the date the tax was paid, whichever is later**. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=49)

These rules cover all the record‑keeping durations you need to observe for federal tax purposes. No other part of the provided context gives a different or more specific time‑frame.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **They allow you to monitor the progress of your business.**  
   Good records let you see whether your business is improving, which products or services are selling well, and where you might need to change strategy. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
2. **They are required to prepare accurate financial statements.**  
   Income statements, balance sheets, cash‑flow statements, and payroll reports all come from the records you keep. These statements are useful for dealing with banks, creditors, and other stakeholders. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
3. **They support the income, expenses, and credits reported on your tax returns.**  
   The IRS can examine your returns at any time; if they ask you to explain an item, a complete set of records will speed the review and reduce the chance of penalties. The records must show how you arrived at the numbers on your return. “Your business records must…support the entries in your books and on your tax return.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
4. **They satisfy federal tax‑record‑keeping requirements and help you stay in compliance.**  
   The Internal Revenue Code requires you to keep records that may be needed for the administration of any provision of the code. “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
5. **They help you meet the IRS’s record‑retention limits.**  
   The period of limitations for an item of income or deduction (e.g., 3, 4, or 6 years) tells you how long you must keep the related documents. Employment‑tax records must be kept for 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
6. **They protect you in potential legal or audit situations.**  
   If the IRS conducts an audit or you face a legal claim, having the supporting documents (invoices, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, payroll records, etc.) allows you to demonstrate that your accounting was correct and that you complied with tax law. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

In short, keeping organized, accurate business records lets you manage your company effectively, file correct tax returns, prove compliance with the IRS, and protect your interests if a dispute arises.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 12)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
The segments explain how a business chooses an accounting method and when certain methods are required.  
In short, you pick either the **cash method** or the **accrual method** (or a combination that follows the rules).  

**Cash method** – Use this if you (1) are a sole‑prop or similar owner‑operator, (2) do *not* keep inventory, and (3) are a small‑business taxpayer. Income is reported when you receive it and expenses are deducted in the year you pay them.  
> "Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier to keep cash method records." [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

**Accrual method** – Required if you must keep inventory or if you have a larger business. Income is reported when earned, and expenses are deducted when incurred, whether or not you actually paid the money that year.  
> "Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the year you earn it … and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them … If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method …" [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

**Combination method** – Allowed only if it clearly shows income and follows the IRS rules (e.g., if inventory is required you must use accrual for purchases and sales; the rest can be cash).  
> "You can generally use any combination of cash, accrual, and special methods … However, if you use the cash method for figuring your income, you must use cash for reporting expenses …" [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

**When you need IRS approval** – If you change the method after your first return, you normally must file Form 3115 (or Form 1128 for tax‑year changes). Small businesses can sometimes get automatic approval.  
> "If you want to change the method ... you must ... generally get IRS approval before you can change to another method." [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

**So, what to do?**  
1. Determine if you have inventory.  
   *If no inventory → cash method is usually simplest.*  
2. If you *do* keep inventory or your business size requires it → accrual method.  
3. If you are a small business and you could count inventory as non‑incidental supplies, you can still use cash.  
   > "Certain small business taxpayers can use the cash method of accounting and can also account for inventoriable items as materials and supplies that are not incidental." [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

4. Once chosen, keep the same method for all tax years unless you file for a change with Form 3115 and receive IRS approval.  

**Summary**  
- **Cash**: no inventory, small business.  
- **Accrual**: inventory is required, or larger business.  
- **Combination**: only if it follows the IRS constraints above.  

Follow the citations above for the precise rules.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)
3. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow a routine self‑inspection process as described in the handbook:

1. **Perform regular safety and health inspections**  
   *Schedule inspections that are frequent enough to capture changes in the workplace, such as new equipment, processes or materials.*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists**  
   *Select the checklists that apply to the areas most critical to your business. These checklists are based on OSHA standards and general safety principles; they provide a starting point for identifying hazards that you can then tailor to your specific work processes.*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Compile related information**  
   *Combine the completed checklists with injury/illness records, training records, and equipment maintenance logs. This helps you see where hazards remain after controls are applied and where new issues may arise.*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

4. **Review and update hazard controls**  
   *After identifying hazards, put in place controls and periodically re‑inspect to confirm the controls are still effective.*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

5. **Engage workers**  
   *Workers should be involved in the inspections, reporting potential hazards, and suggesting control improvements.*  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

6. **Document findings and actions**  
   *Keep records of inspections, the hazards found, the controls applied, and any follow‑up actions needed.*  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

By following these steps—conducting routine self‑inspections, using the handbook checklists, reviewing supporting records, and involving workers—you can systematically identify and manage hazards in your workplace.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 8)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 7)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
**Cash vs Accrual Accounting – What the IRS Says**

| Feature | Cash method | Accrual method |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| **When you report income** | In the year you **receive** the money (or it is constructively received) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) | In the year you **earn** it (when the right to the money is fixed, even if you don’t get paid yet) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |
| **When you report expenses** | In the year you **pay** the bill (or actually spend the cash) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) | In the year you **incur** the cost (when the liability is fixed and can be reasonably measured) – even if you don’t pay it until later [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |
| **Common example** | You get a $500 check on Dec 30, 2025 but can’t deposit it until Jan 3, 2026. You must include it in 2025 income because the check was constructively received in 2025, even though you didn’t have the cash until 2026. That’s the cash‑method rule for receipts [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) | You buy office supplies in December 2025, get the bill that month, but pay it in January 2026. Under accrual you can deduct the expense in 2025 because the liability was fixed and the cost can be determined – you matched the expense to the period when the supplies were used. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Inventory rule** | If you keep an inventory, you **must** use the accrual method for purchases and sales. Small business taxpayers may treat inventories as supplies and still use cash, but it is an exception. | Inventories are always valued on a yearly basis to compute cost of goods sold, so accrual is the default except for very small businesses. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Typical business size** | Many sole‑proprietors and small businesses without inventory use cash because it’s simpler and still allowed. | Businesses that produce, purchase, or sell merchandise usually need accrual because inventory tracks sales and costs. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |
| **Main difference in a nutshell** | Cash = “when you get the money” / “when you pay”  | Accrual = “when you earn the money” / “when you owe it” |

### Why the difference matters

1. **Timing of income & expenses** – The two methods can change the year a dollar is shown, which can affect your tax liability for that year.  
2. **Inventory & cost of goods sold** – Accrual provides a more accurate picture of profits for businesses that sell products, because it matches the cost of the goods sold with the revenue from those goods.  
3. **Simplicity vs precision** – Cash is easier to track for small operators who keep little or no inventory, while accrual gives a better picture for larger or inventory‑heavy businesses.

---

**Bottom line:**  
Under the *cash method* you count money only when you actually touch it; under the *accrual method* you count money when the earnings event occurs, whether or not payment has been made. The choice matters for when you report income, when you deduct expenses, and whether you must keep an inventory.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)
3. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes – you can deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that are directly related to traveling away from your tax home for business purposes.

**What you can deduct**

| Item | How to calculate | Key limits | Source |
|------|-----------------|------------|--------|
| **Transportation to or from a business destination** (air, train, bus, car, taxi, shuttle, etc.) | Actual cost or use the standard mileage rate for a vehicle (70 ¢/mile for 2025) plus any business‑related tolls or parking | You may **not** deduct commuting expenses between your home and your regular workplace | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Lodging (hotel, rentals, etc.)** | Actual cost or the standard meal allowance (see Pub. 463) | Only for overnight or “long enough” stays where sleep or rest is required to perform your job | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Meals** | Actual cost (50 % deductible) or a standard meal allowance | 50 % of meals is usually deductible; you may use the museum's standard allowance instead of actual expenses | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Baggage & shipping** (sending items between locations) | Actual cost | Must be ordinary and necessary for business | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Vehicle expenses** (operating, maintenance, insurance, parking, tolls) | Actual expenses **or** standard mileage rate (75 ¢/mile for 2025) | If you elect standard mileage, you can still deduct business‑related parking, tolls, and interest on a car loan | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Miscellaneous** (telephone, tips, cleaning) | Actual cost | Must be ordinary and necessary | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |

**Requirements for a deductible business trip**

1. **Away from your tax home**: Your duties must require you to be substantially farther from your regular workplace than a normal day’s work and you must need sleep or rest while away.  
2. **Ordinary and necessary**: The expense is common in your trade and helps you perform duties.  
3. **Keep records**: You must maintain receipts and log business purpose and miles.  

**Summary**

You can deduct travel expenses such as transport, lodging, meals (50 %) and vehicle costs (actual or standard mileage) when the trip meets the “away‑from‑home” test. Record each expense and keep documentation to back up the deduction.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 41)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 40)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)
3. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 35)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)
4. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
The executive summary is a concise, one‑ to two‑paragraph snapshot that readers can skim for the key take‑away. It should:

* **State the business idea** – what you’re selling or providing and why it matters.  
* **Outline the financial need and funding use** – how much capital you’re seeking, what it will cover (start‑up costs, working capital, etc.), and how much you’ve already invested.  
* **Give a high‑level timeline of milestones** – when you expect to hit major goals such as product launch, first revenue, break‑even, etc.  
* **Be brief and to the point** – keep it short, clear, and compelling; write it last so you can reference the details in the rest of the plan.  

These elements should be captured in one or two paragraphs that give a quick but complete picture of your business and its growth prospects.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market you should follow this outline:

1. **Identify the niche** – state who your best customers are.  
   - For a business market, break them down by industry, company size, location, or how they use the product.  
   - For a consumer (household) market, segment by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.  
   *Source: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)*  

2. **Give clear characteristics** – list the key traits that define each segment (e.g., “18‑35 year‑old urban professionals with disposable income”).  
   *Source: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)*  

3. **Estimate size and growth** – use population figures, industry reports, sales‑tax data, or other statistics to gauge the approximate size of each segment and its potential growth.  
   *Source: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)*  

4. **Show how much of the market you will capture** – state a realistic percentage of the total market you expect to serve.  
   *Source: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)*  

**Example**  
> “Our target market is urban, tech‑savvy professionals aged 25–40 who work in software development and are willing to pay a premium for eco‑friendly office supplies. According to the 2023 U.S. Census, there are roughly 5 million such professionals in the Seattle metro area, a market that is projected to grow 3 % annually.”

This structure gives a concise yet complete description of your target market.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes – because your shop is a **public accommodation** (a private business that sells goods or services to the public), the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires you to remove physical barriers that are **readily achievable**.  
If you can adapt the shop so people who use wheelchairs can enter, move around, and access your services, you must do so. If a change is *not* readily achievable, the ADA allows you to provide an alternative method (e.g., phone orders, curb‑side pickup, or delivery) and to keep the business open to all customers, not just people with disabilities.  

**What the ADA requires for existing facilities**

- **Existing facilities are not exempt**; you cannot simply rely on a “grandfather” exception.  When a business serves the public, it must comply with the ADA’s accessibility obligations for existing facilities.  The goal is to remove barriers that are “readily achievable” (i.e., can be done without extreme difficulty or expense) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).

- **Barrier removal must be “readily achievable.”**  The definition depends on the size, type, and resources of your business.  Large businesses are expected to remove more barriers than small ones, and you can defer changes if you lack funds, but the obligation remains in the future as resources become available [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).

- **Key areas you must address first** –  
    * **Entrance** – a clear, accessible entrance (e.g., width ≥36 in., a ramp with slope ≤1:12, handrails, and a 30×48 in. clear floor space in front of any counter if the counter is not accessible) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
    * **Doors** – door hardware must be operable without grasping (lever handles, loop‑type handles).  Narrow revolving turnstiles must be replaced or bypassed [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13).  
    * **Aisles & maneuvering space** – 36‑in. wide aisles, at least 3 ft. by 3 ft. turning space, 30×48 in. clearance in front of counters, and 30 in. by 48 in. clearance at fixed seating or tables.  Shelving should be placed so they don’t block an accessible route [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17).  
    * **Market or service counters** – if a counter is higher than 36 in., provide a lowered section that is at least 36 in. long and no higher than 36 in. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
    * **Parking** – provide at least one accessible parking space (and, if total spaces ≤25, that space must also be van‑accessible) on level ground and an accessible route without steps or steep slopes [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9).

- **If a barrier cannot be removed readily**, you may provide an alternative method for access to goods and services (e.g., phone orders, curb‑side pickup, delivery, or a separate accessible area) and you must publicize that alternative [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).

**Bottom line**

- **You do have to make your shop wheelchair accessible** if it can be done without a prohibitive cost or structural change.  
- If any element (door, aisle, counter, parking, entrance) is not readily achievable, you must still allow people with disabilities to access your services through alternative means and disclose those alternatives.

The ADA’s purpose is to ensure that everyone can use your shop in a way that is safe and convenient, so start by examining the specific accessibility elements listed above and plan the changes that are “readily achievable” for your business.

results.question: how many employees before ada employment rules apply
results.answer:
The ADA employment rules apply to businesses that have **15 or more employees**. This threshold is the point at which the EEOC begins to provide technical assistance on ADA employment requirements. results.question: how long do i have to report a workplace death
results.answer:
All work‑related fatalities must be reported to OSHA **within 8 hours** of the incident. results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You are exempt from OSHA injury‑recordkeeping only if you meet the specific conditions listed in the regulations. According to the guidance you provided, employers are *partially exempt* from the requirement to keep OSHA Forms 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) and 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report) **if:**

1. **All employees** in the employer’s business were **ten or fewer** during each month of the entire last calendar year; or   
2. The employer operates in a **low‑hazard industry** as defined in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.  

Even if you qualify for this exemption, you must still **report** all work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye to OSHA within the required time periods [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

results.question: how long do i keep injury records
results.answer:
You must retain OSHA injury records for at least five years.  
The OSHA Form 300 (log), Form 301 (incident report), and Form 300A (annual summary) must be kept at the worksite for a minimum of five years.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

results.answer:
**What you must keep and for how long** | Type of records | What to keep | How long to keep | Source | |-----------------|--------------|-----------------|--------| | **Tax‑related records** | • Supporting documents that back up each item of income and deduction reported on your return (sales slips, invoices, bank deposit slips, canceled checks, receipts, payroll records, etc.).
• Copies of each tax return you filed (and any amended returns).

• Asset‑related records (purchase price, depreciation, sale details, Section 179 elections, casualty losses) to compute basis and gain/loss when the asset is sold or otherwise disposed of. | • For general business records, keep them **as long as any period of limitations for that return has not expired** – typically **3 years** from the filing date, but longer if the return is amended or if you owe additional tax (see Table 3 in the IRS limits).
• **Employment‑tax records**: keep **4 years** after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.
• **Asset records**: keep them until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the asset in a taxable transaction.
• Keep all copies of filed returns unchanged; you may destroy the originals only if an electronic record‐keeping system is in place and has been tested for compliance. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) | | **Injury & illness records (OSHA)** | • **OSHA Form 300** (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) for all recordable injuries.
• **OSHA Form 301** (Injury and Illness Incident Report) for every recordable case.
• **OSHA Form 300A** (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) – annual summary filed with OSHA.
• Any supplementary incident details required for Form 301 (e.g., medical records, employee statements).
• If you have 100+ workers in a high‑hazard industry or meet the OSHA reporting thresholds, you must also electronically submit the Form 300A summary. | • Keep **OSHA Forms 300, 301, and 300A at the worksite for at least 5 years**.
• The supplemental incident records used for Form 301 must be retained for the period required for that specific record (e.g., medical records as dictated by state law or employer policy).
• Electronic submission of the Form 300A summary must be made annually by **March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered by the forms** if your establishment meets the size or industry thresholds. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15), [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) | ### How to meet the retention requirements - **For tax records**—Keep all supporting documents (in hard‑copy or electronically) in an organized, legible system. If you shift to electronic storage, the system must preserve, index, retrieve, and reproduce the records in a legible format and must be fully test‑verified by the IRS. See the guidelines for electronic storage systems in Segment 2. - **For injury records**—Store the forms in a secure place at the worksite, protect them from loss or damage, and maintain them for the full five‑year period. If you are required to submit the Form 300A electronically to OSHA, do so by the March 2 deadline for each year. These are the specific records and retention periods that the IRS and OSHA require for a small business owner. results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
To keep your employees safe **and** make sure the premises can be accessed by people with disabilities, you need a coordinated, written safety‐and‑access program that covers the following key areas:

| What you should do | Why it matters | Where it is stated in the handbook |
|---------------------|----------------|-------------------------------------|
| **1. Create a safety‑and‑health program** – management must lead it, involve workers, identify hazards, train and review it often. | A strong program reduces injuries, saves on insurance and legal costs, and builds a safer culture. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) describes the seven core elements; [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9) lists the required activities (reporting, inspections, training). |
| **2. Conduct regular workplace inspections** – check walkways, equipment, and the access route to see if they remain safe. | Spotting a new step, a wet floor, or a clogged door before a worker reaches it prevents accidents. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79) and [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78) give detailed clearance, cleaning, and repair requirements for walking‑working surfaces. |
| **3. Keep walkways clear and wide** – at least 36 in. for wheelchair maneuvering, 30 × 48 in. clear space in front of counters, and 3‑ft turning space for aisles. | Employees – especially those in wheelchairs – can move freely without tripping or slipping. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73) – aisles, shelves, and counters; [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) – in‑store aisles and turning spaces. |
| **4. Make entrances accessible** – a ramp (max 1:12 slope), side‑handrails (if rise > 6 in.), landing 18‑in. beyond the door, edge protection, and a clear route to the door. | People with mobility aids can enter without a step, and the route is usable in all weather. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10), [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) (ramp width ≥ 36 in., landing ≥ 18 in.), [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) (32‑in. opening if a turnstile is removed). |
| **5. Replace or add accessible gates next to turnstiles** – if a turnstile is required, the adjacent gate must be at least 32 in. wide. | Wheelchair users, walkers, or cane users cannot push through narrow turnstiles. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) details turning‑gate width requirements. |
| **6. Install signage** that points to the accessible entrance when a building has a non‑accessible primary door. | People who can’t use the primary entrance immediately see where to go. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) – “a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance”. |
| **7. Provide accessible parking** – sign with the international symbol, 5‑ft aisle (or 8‑ft for vans), and a level access path to the building entrance. | Employees and customers arriving by car can reach the building without stairs or steps. | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) (parking spaces, aisle width), [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) (signage, routing). |
| **8. Install and maintain safe exit routes** – at least two exits from elevated areas, exit signs 6 in. high, emergency lighting, and a clear chain of command for evacuations. | In a fire or other emergency, everyone can evacuate quickly and safely. | [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26) (evacuation plan, exit signage), [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28) (evidence of exit signs), [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54) (exits listed). |
| **9. Protect workers from falling hazards** – guardrails, safety nets, headroom, and PPE for any elevated work. | Falls are among the most common serious injuries in small businesses. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73) (guardrails, safety nets, PPE). |
| **10. Keep machinery and equipment safe** – clean, maintenance, lockout, manual controls, emergency stop buttons. | Prevents accidental starts, burns or other equipment‑related injuries. | [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54) (equipment safety checklist). |
| **11. | **12. results.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
results.answer:
**How to write a business plan**

1. **Cover page** – put the company name, address, phone number, owners’ contact info, logo, and date of the plan.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

2. **Table of contents** – optional, but useful for long plans.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

3. **Executive summary** – a concise one‑to‑two‑paragraph overview that tells the reader what the business is, how much money you need, where the money will go, and a short schedule of goals.  Draft this last.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

4. **Business description** – describe the product/service, how it gives you a sustainable competitive advantage, the regulations that apply, the facilities and equipment you need, and the overall industry outlook.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

5. **Management plan** – outline the organizational structure, list owners and their ownership percentages, and describe key managers’ responsibilities, qualifications and day‑to‑day duties.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

6. **Market analysis** – estimate the total market, focus on your target market, analyze competition, and explain how you will make and promote your product/service.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

7. **Financial (money) section** – present the startup cost summary, a 3‑year income projection, a statement of cash flow, a balance sheet, and a break‑even analysis.  Include supporting documents such as your “Sources and Uses” sheet and notes on critical assumptions.  The SBDC can help you prepare these four key documents.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  

8. **Exhibits** – attach resumes, purchase agreements, bids, contracts, floor plans, or any other document that substantiates what is written in the plan.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

9. **Review and refine** – ask a mentor, accountant, or SCORE/SBDC advisor to review the plan and provide feedback before finalizing.  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  


**Setting up accounting**

1. **Choose a legal and tax structure** – decide on sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, or LLC, obtain an EIN if you’ll have employees, and file the appropriate formation documents (articles of incorporation, name registration, etc.).  
   [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  

2. **Open a dedicated business checking account** – keep it separate from personal funds, use it for all deposits and withdrawals, and keep the account address in your business records.  
   [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

3. **Use a business checkbook / register** – record each expense the day it occurs, note the source of each receipt, and write checks only for documented expenditures.  Avoid paying cash unless you keep a proper receipt and note the reason.  
   [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

4. **Decide on an accounting method**  
   * **Cash method** – record income when received and expenses when paid (often used if you have no inventory).  
   * **Accrual method** – record income when earned and expenses when incurred (required if you keep inventory or have significant accounts receivable).  
   * You may need IRS approval to change methods.  
   [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

5. **Pick a bookkeeping system**  
   * **Single‑entry** – simple, tracks income and expenses with daily and monthly cash receipt

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
Yes, you need an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if your business

* hires one or more employees, or  
* must file pension or excise‑tax returns, or  
* chooses to use an EIN instead of its owner’s Social‑Security number for tax‑identification purposes.  

These requirements are stated in the IRS publication excerpts: *“If you must have an EIN, include it along with your SSN on your Schedule C (Form 1040) as instructed.”* and *“You must also have an EIN to use as a TIN if you do either of the following… Pay wages to one or more employees. File pension or excise tax returns.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)【5】.  
Even when you are a sole proprietor with no employees, you may still obtain an EIN; the publication notes: *“If your business will hire employees or pay Federal Excise Tax, a Federal Employer’s Identification Number (EIN) must be obtained.”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)【18】.  

**What accounting method do you choose?**  
An EIN does not dictate a particular accounting method.  When you file your first income‑tax return, you must choose an accounting method—**cash** or **accrual** (or a special/combination method if required).  

* Cash method: report income in the year it is received and match expenses to the year they are paid.  
* Accrual method: report income in the year it is earned and match expenses to the year they are incurred, whether or not you pay them then.  

If you have inventory that must be accounted for, the default rule is to use an accrual method for purchases and sales; a small‑business taxpayer may use a cash method for inventory that is treated as “non‑incidental material or supplies.”  (See *“If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for purchases and sales.”* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) and *“If you are a small business taxpayer, you can choose not to keep an inventory, but you must still use a method of accounting for inventory that clearly reflects income.”* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)​).

Thus, you can apply for an EIN at any time that meets the above criteria, and you choose your accounting method independently—most small businesses with no inventory use the cash method, while businesses that maintain inventory typically use the accrual method unless the small‑business exception applies.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 6)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
results.answer:
You must keep the OSHA injury‑and‑illness records that your business is required to file.  
- **OSHA Form 300** – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses  
- **OSHA Form 301** – Injury and Illness Incident Report (a supplementary record for each recordable case)  
- **OSHA Form 300A** – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses  

These forms must be kept at the worksite for a minimum of **five years** after the date they are recorded. This retention period applies to the 300, 301, and 300A records.

results.question: do i need workers comp insurance and can i deduct it
results.answer:
**Do you need workers’ compensation insurance?**  
Yes.  Workers’ compensation insurance is required by state law for any employee that can be injured on the job, and the law requires you to carry it whenever you have employees.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37)  

**Can you deduct the premiums you pay?**  
Yes.  Premiums for workers’ compensation insurance are deductible as a business expense on Schedule C (Form 1040).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37)  

(If you’re unsure whether your particular state requires it, the state Department of Labor website is a reliable reference.)

results.question: what if a customer cannot get through my front door and what if someone is hurt on site
results.answer:
**If a customer cannot get through your front‑door entrance**

1. **Give them an alternative accessible entrance** – if the main door is not usable, you must provide another publicly‑accessible entrance that is compliant with the ADA.  
   *The ADA requires that: “When one entrance is not accessible and another entrance is accessible, a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance.  The alternative entrance must be open during store hours.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

2. **Clear signage and lighting** – place a sign that clearly points from the main entrance to the alternative entrance.  The sign should be mounted at an accessible height (generally ≤ 48 in. above the ground).  If a security gate keeps the alternative door locked, install a buzzer or call‑bell that is positioned on an accessible route and is no more than 48 in. tall.  The “buzzer or call bell” must be placed so a wheelchair user can reach it. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

3. **Keep the alternative door unlocked during business hours** – the door that serves as the secondary entrance must remain unlocked.  If the door can’t be kept unlocked for security reasons, provide a door‑open system (unlocked handle, call box, etc.) that is accessible. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

4. **If the main entry has a turnstile** – remove the turnstile or replace it with an accessible gate.  The opening must be at least 32 in. wide (or as wide as practicable) and must be left open during hours. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)  

5. **Re‑evaluate the main entrance** – where possible, modify the existing door: add a ramp, eliminate a single step, or reinstall a lever handle so that the primary door itself becomes accessible.  These modifications are lower‑cost ways to avoid reliance on a secondary entrance. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

---

**If someone is hurt on the site**

1. **First‑aid readiness** – the site must have a fully supplied first‑aid kit that is easy to reach from each area and is inspected and replenished regularly.  At least one worker on each shift must be trained and qualified to render first aid.  If a medical facility is not nearby, you must have first‑aid trained staff and the required protective gear. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=62)  

2. **Medical personnel** – if staff are expected to respond to medical emergencies, they should receive first‑aid training, hepatitis B vaccination, and be trained on universal precautions. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=62)  

3. **Record‑keeping** – record all occupational injuries (except trivial first‑aid‑only cases) on OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses).  For each recordable incident, file Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report).  At year‑end, produce Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses).  Employers with 250+ workers, or 20–249 in high‑hazard industries, must file Form 300A electronically by **March 2** of the following year. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  

4. **Reporting serious incidents** – any fatality, in‑patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye must be reported to OSHA immediately.  

5. **Emergency planning** – maintain a written workplace‑violence and emergency plan that includes clear procedures for calling security or police, and drill the staff on what to do if an injury occurs.  OSHA recommends that all employees be trained on the emergency program. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=85)  

By following the above steps you will ensure that customers who cannot use the front door are still able to enter and that any on‑site injuries are handled promptly, safely, and in compliance with OSHA record‑keeping requirements.

results.question: how much cash before i have to report it and do i need a licence to serve food
results.answer:
You must report large cash takings and you need a food‑service license if you intend to prepare and serve food.

**Cash reporting**

* If you receive **more than $10,000 in cash in a single transaction, or in two or more related business transactions,** you are required to file **Form 8300, “Report of Cash Payments Over $10,000 Received in a Trade or Business.”**  
  *Cash includes U.S. and foreign coin and currency, as well as cashier’s checks, traveler’s checks and money orders. Personal checks are not counted.*  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  

**License to serve food**

* Any business that prepares and serves food must first have its premises inspected by the local **Health Department**. Only after that inspection can a **food license** (or a lodging license, if the business also provides lodging) be issued.  
* If you plan to sell alcohol, you will need separate liquor, beer or wine licenses from your local city or county government.  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=8)  

So: report cash when you cross the $10,000 threshold with Form 8300, and obtain a health‑department food license (and possibly an alcohol license) before serving food.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 12)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)

results.question: why should i bother with a safety program and what records do i need to keep
results.answer:
A safety program is a worthwhile investment because it protects workers, keeps the business compliant, and saves money.  In the handbook it is described as a way to “prevent workplace injuries and illnesses, improve compliance with laws and regulations, reduce costs (including significant reductions in workers’‑compensation premiums), engage workers, enhance social‑responsibility goals, and increase productivity and overall business operations” – all of which are highlighted as benefits of a safety and health program [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6).

In addition, a safety program must be documented and maintained.  The handbook specifies the records you must keep and how long to keep them:

* **Injury and illness records** – Every recordable injury or illness (except minor first‑aid cases) is entered on OSHA Form 300, and a detailed Incident Report is filed on OSHA Form 301.  These records must be kept at the worksite for at least five years [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
* **Summary records** – At the end of each calendar year you must prepare an annual summary on OSHA Form 300A.  For businesses that need to report (see below) the summary must be electronically submitted to OSHA by **March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered** [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
* **Medical and exposure records** – Worker medical records and exposure records must be retained for the period required for each specific type of record, and must be accessible to workers as required by OSHA [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
* **Training records** – Records of safety and health training (including worker‑specific training) must be kept and must be easily reviewable by workers [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
* **Fatalities and severe injuries** – All work‑related fatalities must be reported to OSHA within **8 hours**, and all hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye must be reported within **24 hours** [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  

Reporting requirements vary by business size and industry:

* If your establishment has **100 or more workers** in a high‑hazard industry, you must electronically submit Form 300A by March 2 [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
* If you have **250 or more workers** (or 20–249 workers in certain high‑rate industries) you are also required to submit Form 300A by March 2 [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).  
* Employers with **10 or fewer workers** (or in certain low‑hazard industries) are partially exempt from these record‑keeping rules [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).  

Keeping these records demonstrates compliance, supports investigation of incidents, and helps you track safety performance.  The handbook makes clear that a written safety program, regular self‑inspections, and proper record‑keeping together create a culture of safety that protects workers and the business alike [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7).

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
The IRS requires you to keep records for the length of time that they might be needed to show, compute, or verify your tax return.  The general rule is to retain records “until the period of limitations for that return runs out.”  Tables of those limitation periods are in the IRS guidance (see the “Table 3 – Period of Limitations” mentioned in the text).  Typical periods are:

| What you’re keeping | Typical retention period |
|---------------------|--------------------------|
| **General income‑tax records** (e.g., receipts, invoices, payroll records, copies of filed returns) | 3 years, unless an exception applies (4 months for records relating to an audit that started after the following period, 6 years for some deduction claims, 7 years for fraudulent returns, etc.) – the exact period is given in “Table 3”【Segment 1】 |
| **Employment‑tax records** (payroll information, forms W‑2, W‑3, 941/944, etc.) | 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later【Segment 1】 |
| **Asset records** (purchase invoices, depreciation schedules, sale documents) | Keep records until the period of limitations expires for the year you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition【Segment 1】 |
| **Other non‑tax uses** (e.g., insurance, creditor requirements) | Even after the IRS period lapses, don’t discard records until you know no other party needs them【Segment 1】 |

**Important points**

* Keep copies of your filed tax returns.  They aid future returns and any amended returns【Segment 1】.  
* The 4‑year rule for employment taxes applies only when payroll tax records are involved【Segment 1】.  
* For asset‑related records, the limitation period begins in the year you sell or otherwise dispose of the property, not when you originally bought it【Segment 1】.  

If you’re unsure which period applies to a specific record, consult the IRS table of limitations, or keep the record longer to satisfy any other legal or contractual obligations.

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records for several concrete reasons:

- **Support your tax filings** – The IRS requires you to have documentation that backs up every income and deduction you report. Records such as sales slips, receipts, bank deposits, and canceled checks are the proof you can provide if the IRS questions a return. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
- **Enable accurate tax reporting** – A clear record‑keeping system lets you compile the figures that go on your tax return and ensures you claim the correct deductions. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
- **Help you manage the business** – Good records let you monitor how the business is doing (sales trends, expenses, cash flow) and help you prepare financial statements that banks, investors, or creditors may request. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
- **Meet legal and regulatory deadlines** – You must retain records that could be needed for the administration of the Internal Revenue Code, usually until the applicable statute of limitations expires (often 3–7 years, depending on the item). [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Provide evidence in disputes or audits** – If the IRS or another government agency asks to examine your records, having them ready speeds up the process and gives you a better chance to prove the accuracy of your return. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

In short, keeping business records is essential for tax compliance, financial management, and legal protection.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
**Which accounting method to choose**

1. **Cash method**  
   • If you do **not have inventory** and your business is not a manufacturer, retailer, or producer of goods that need inventory tracking, the cash method is normally the simplest and is allowed for most sole‑proprietors and partnerships.  
   • You record income when you receive the money and record expenses when you actually pay them.  
   • The cash method is allowed for most people who keep no inventory, but if you later start holding inventory you’ll need to change to an accrual method.  
   – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

2. **Accrual method**  
   • If your business **must maintain inventory** to account for sales and purchases (e.g., you sell goods, manufacturers, wholesalers), you must generally use an accrual method for those purchases and sales.  The accrual method records income when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash moves.  
   – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

3. **Special treatment for small businesses**  
   • A small‑business taxpayer (average annual gross receipts $31 million or less for the prior three years) can **use the cash method and still treat inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies**.  
   – [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

4. **Combination or special methods**  
   • You may combine cash and accrual elements (e.g., accrual for inventory, cash for other items) as long as the overall method clearly shows income and is applied consistently.  
   – [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  
   • You can also use special methods (e.g., depreciation, installment sales) for particular items of income or expense.  
   – [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

5. **Changing methods**  
   • Once you have chosen a method, you generally need IRS approval to change it (File Form 1128 for the tax year, or Form 3115 for inventory methods).  
   – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)

**Bottom line**  
- Choose **cash** if your business has no inventory and you want the simplest method.  
- Choose **accrual** (or a combination that includes accrual for inventory) if you keep inventory.  
- Small businesses can still use cash even with inventory, provided they treat that inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies.  

If you later decide to switch, be sure to apply for IRS approval using the appropriate forms.

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To find and fix hazards in your workplace, follow these steps:

1. **Start with a routine self‑inspection**  
   * Have knowledgeable workers walk through the work area and look for anything that could cause injury or illness.  This is the only way to know whether a hazard exists and whether it is being controlled.  The handbook says a self‑inspection “identifies hazards, controls identified hazards, and monitors and evaluates hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Use a workplace self‑inspection checklist**  
   * The handbook provides checklists that cover common industry hazards (e.g., walking‑working surfaces, storage, confined spaces).  Pick the checklists that apply to your business and fill them out during the inspection. The completed checklists are the starting point for deciding what actions to take.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

3. **Combine checklist data with other records**  
   * After you add the checklist results, bring in injury/illness logs, maintenance records, and any equipment failure reports.  This combined picture helps you spot patterns that show which hazards are still a problem.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

4. **Match identified hazards to OSHA standards**  
   * Review the OSHA rules that apply to your industry (general industry: 29 CFR 1910, construction: 1926, etc.).  The handbook helps you see whether a particular hazard is covered by a standard or whether it falls under the general duty clause.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

5. **Control the hazards**  
   * For each identified hazard, decide on a control: engineering (e.g., guardrails, ventilation), administrative (e.g., job rotation, training), or personal protective equipment (PPE).  The checklist and the program sections highlight the kinds of controls you should use.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=69)

6. **Get help if you need it**  
   * OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation Program offers free, confidential visits by safety professionals who can help you conduct a thorough hazard assessment and recommend fixes.  You can request a visit for a single concern or a full‑facility review.  [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

7. **Document and review**  
   * Keep the inspection reports, hazard‑control plans, training records, and any changes you make.  Review the program each year (or whenever conditions change) to make sure controls still work.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

8. **Keep workers informed**  
   * Make sure workers know what they saw in the inspection, why a hazard matters, and how they can help keep the workplace safe.  HR or safety teams can give short briefings or use posted signs.  [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=5)

9. **Post required safety information**  
   * The OSHA poster and summary of injuries/illnesses must be displayed in a visible place, required by the program guidelines.  This keeps everyone aware that hazard control matters.  [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=13)

Using these steps, you’ll have a repeatable, documented process that finds hazards, checks that they’re being controlled, and shows you where improvements are needed.
