runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash‑method accounting records money when it actually moves.  
- Income is included in a tax year when you **receive** it (or when it becomes constructively received).  
- Expenses are deducted in the year you **pay** them, unless special rules apply.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

Accrual‑method accounting matches income and expenses to the year they are earned or incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands.  
- Income is reported in the year it is **earned** (e.g., a sale is earned when the product is delivered or the service is performed, even if payment comes later).  
- Expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year they are **incurred** (when the obligation is created, even if payment is made later).  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

**Key differences**

| | Cash method | Accrual method |
|---|---|---|
|Income timing|When cash is received (or constructively available) |When earned (when the right to receive is fixed) |
|Expense timing|When cash is paid |When liability is incurred (all‑events test) |
|Best for small businesses with no inventory or simple cash flow |Used when inventory must be tracked or when income/expenditure patterns are more complex |  

For example, if you furnish a client and invoice them in December but receive payment in January, cash method would include the income in January, while accrual method includes it in December. Similarly, if you buy supplies in December but pay the supplier in January, cash method would deduct the expense in January, whereas accrual method would deduct it in December.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

So, the essential difference is **when** the tax returns count the money—cash method counts when the money moves, accrual method counts when the business activity (income or expense) takes place.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes – you can deduct the ordinary and necessary expenses that you incur while traveling for your business.  The deduction is limited to costs that relate to travel “away from home” (your tax home) for a length of time that requires sleep or rest and that are required by your business duties and are not personal or vacation expenses.  The following excerpts explain what you can deduct and the limits that apply:

**1.  General eligibility for travel deductions**  
- Travel expenses are deductible when you are away from your tax home for substantially longer than a day’s work **and** need sleep or rest to perform your duties. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  

**2.  Meals and lodging**  
- You may deduct the cost of meals and lodging on an overnight business trip.  You may choose to use actual expenses or the standard meal allowance, but in most cases you can deduct only 50 % of meals. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  

**3.  Transportation**  
- Deduct the cost of traveling by air, train, bus, or car between your home and a business destination.  
- Taxpayers can also deduct taxi, commuter bus, and limousine fares between the airport or station and the hotel or between the hotel and the work location.  
- For car or truck travel you can deduct either actual expenses (fuel, oil, insurance, parking, tolls, depreciation, etc.) or the standard mileage rate (70 ¢ per mile in 2025; 72.5 ¢ per mile in 2026).  If you elect the standard rate, you may still deduct business‑related parking fees and tolls, but not other car expenses or insurance. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=36)  

**4.  Local vs. overnight travel**  
- Local business transportation (moving between two workplaces in the same city or general area) is not deductible; only travel that takes you away from your tax home overnight is deductible. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)  

**5.  Reimbursing employees**  
- When you reimburse employees for travel and meal expenses, the amount you deduct depends on whether the reimbursement is provided under an accountable or non‑accountable plan. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  

**6.  General limitations**  
- Only ordinary and necessary expenses qualify.  
- The deduction is not available for expenses that are mainly for personal use, for vacations, or for commuting between your home and your regular workplace. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=42)  

So, if your travel meets the “away‑from‑home” criteria, you can deduct the related transportation costs, 50 % of the meals, lodging, and any allowable parking or tolls, using either the actual‑expense or standard‑mileage methods for vehicle expenses.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 40)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 41)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

runs.question: what goes in an executive summary
runs.answer:
The executive summary is the first, and often only, section many readers look at, so it should give a concise snapshot of your business plan.  It should be one or two short paragraphs that cover:

* The core business idea – what you’re selling or the service you’re offering.  
* The amount of capital you need, what the money will be used for, and how much you’ll inject yourself or other investors will bring in.  
* A brief schedule of your key milestones and goals.  

Write this section last, after the rest of the plan is complete, so you can reference the exact figures and timelines you’ve detailed elsewhere [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
You can describe your target market by following the steps outlined in the guide:

1. **Define the niche** – state the type of customer that is your “best” buyer.  
   *Is your business selling to small retailers, to tech‑savvy millennials, to business‑to‑business engineering firms, etc.?*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Identify key characteristics** – list demographic, geographic, psychographic, or behavioral traits that define that niche.  
   *For a consumer market, you might note age range, gender, income level, lifestyle, or the specific benefit they seek. For a business market, you might note industry, company size, location, or how the product is used.*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Segment further if needed** – break the market into smaller groups (e.g., “urban millennials earning $50k–$80k who value eco‑friendly products”).  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Estimate market size and growth** – use population data, industry reports, sales‑tax information, or other reliable sources to approximate how many potential customers exist in each segment and how that number is expected to grow.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Project market share** – indicate what portion of the total market you realistically expect to capture in the short and long term.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

**Example**  
*Your best customer is small‑to‑mid‑size retail stores located in urban suburbs that look for high‑margin, eco‑friendly packaging. In 2025 there are roughly 35,000 such stores in the U.S.; projections show a 4% annual growth over the next five years. Your business plans to capture 2% of this segment (≈700 stores) within three years.*  

Use this structure to clearly convey who your target market is, why they matter, and how large and promising the market opportunity is.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  
Because a shop is a **public accommodation**—any private business that provides goods or services to the public—the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires you to remove what the law calls “barriers” that are **readily achievable** and to keep at least one entrance, entrance route, and sales‑area accessible if you can do so without undue expense. The ADA does not exempt existing facilities that were built before 1993; that “grandfather” rule only relaxes the *scope* of the changes that must be made, not the fact that they must be made.  

**Key points from the segments**

1. **Obligation to comply** – “If you own, operate, lease, or lease to a business that serves the public, then, you are covered by the ADA and have obligations for existing facilities as well as for compliance when a facility is altered or a new facility is constructed.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
2. **No “grandfather” exemption** – “Existing facilities are not exempted by ‘grandfather provisions’ that are often used by building code officials.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
3. **Barriers that must be removed** – “If you own or operate a business that serves the public you must remove physical ‘barriers’ that are ‘readily achievable,’ which means…” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
4. **Accessible entrance requirement** – “ …the shop must have at least one accessible entrance… a sign must provide direction to an accessible entrance if another entrance is not accessible.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  
5. **Accessible sales and service areas** – “…If sales or service counters are provided, the counters must be accessible, if doing so is readily achievable.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  
6. **Accessible aisle and parking** – “A wide accessible route must be provided between the accessible entrance and the accessible parking spaces; the parking spaces must have an access aisle.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9)  

**What you need to do**

- Verify whether your shop’s existing entrance, interior aisles, sales counter, and parking area can be made accessible with changes that are *readily achievable* (i.e., can be done without extraordinary expense or structural change).  
- If it is readily achievable, you must make those changes so customers who use wheelchairs can enter, move around, purchase, and exit the shop.  
- If a barrier is not “readily achievable,” you still must provide an alternative accessible service (e.g., staff can assist with items, or offer delivery or curb‑side pickup) until the barrier can be removed.  
- Document the changes and keep a record of any alternative services you provide.

**Parts not covered by the segments**

The segments do not specify exact cost limits or detailed timing for making a shop fully compliant, nor do they describe tax‑credit or deduction options that can offset the costs. Those are covered in other sections not included here.

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
You may be exempt from OSHA’s injury‑ and illness‑recordkeeping rules under two specific circumstances:

* **Size exemption** – If you had **10 or fewer employees during every day of the last calendar year** you are *partially* exempt from keeping OSHA Form 300 logs and Form 301 incident reports.  
 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

* **Industry exemption** – If your work is in a **low‑hazard industry** listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A, you may also be exempt.  
 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

Even when exempt, employers must still:

* **Report** work‑related fatalities; in‑patient hospitalizations; amputations; and loss of an eye to OSHA within 8 hours or 24 hours as required.  
 [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=48)

* **Submit** an annual summary (OSHA Form 300A) electronically by March 2 of the year after the covered calendar year **if** the business has 250+ workers or 20‑249 workers in a high‑hazard industry.  
 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

So, if your business had ≤10 workers all year or operates in one of the designated low‑hazard industries, you are exempt from maintaining the detailed OSHA injury/illness logs—but you still must report severe incidents and may need to file the annual summary depending on size and industry.



**Sources:**

runs.question: how long do i keep injury records
runs.answer:
The OSHA injury and illness recordkeeping requirements specify that a business must retain the following records for **at least five (5) years**:

- OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)  
- OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report)  
- OSHA Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)  

The records must be kept at the worksite (or in a secure electronic system that can be accessed by OSHA) for that minimum period.  
They must also be electronically submitted to OSHA by **March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered** if the employer’s size and industry require it.  
These rules apply to all employers that are required to keep OSHA injury and illness records. If you are an employer with 10 or fewer workers for the entire previous calendar year, you may be partially exempt, but you still must keep fatality, hospitalization, amputation, and eye‑loss records and report them to OSHA within the required time frames.

runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**What records you must keep**

| Purpose | What you keep | How long you keep it | Source |
|---------|---------------|----------------------|--------|
| **General business tax records** – receipts, invoices, bank statements, payroll, depreciation schedules, etc. – that support every item of income, deduction and credit on your returns | All supporting documents that back up your tax‑return entries—sales slips, paid bills, canceled checks, bank deposit slips, payroll records, etc. | “as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code. Generally, this means you must keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out.”  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) | 
| **Copies of filed tax returns** | The printed or electronic copies of every return you file (Form 1040, Schedule C, 941, 940, 1099‑etc.) | “Keep copies of your filed tax returns.”  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) | 
| **Employment‑tax records** (payroll, withholding, FUTA, etc.) | W‑2s, W‑4s, payroll journals, FICA calculation sheets, unemployment‑tax records, etc. | “If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.”  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) | 
| **Property and asset records** (depreciation, sale documents) | Purchase invoices, appraisals, depreciation worksheets, sale agreements, closing statements, etc. | “Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition.”  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) | 
| **General records for state/city/industry reporting** (e.g., payroll reports, sick‑leave logs, safety‑training logs) | Employee compensation, insurance statements, training certificates, etc. | Not specified in the excerpts. | 

**What you keep for injuries / OSHA recordkeeping**

| OSHA form | What you record | How long you keep it | Source |
|-----------|----------------|----------------------|--------|
| **OSHA Form 300 – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** | A daily log of each recordable injury or illness. | “are kept at the worksite for at least five years.”  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 301 – Incident Report** | A detailed incident report for each recordable case. | Same – “at least five years.”  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 300A – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** | An annual summary of the year’s recordable injuries/illnesses. | Same – “at least five years.”  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** | Medical notes, exposure histories, etc. | “are retained for the time period required for each specific type of record.”  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Annual OSHA submission** | The electronic copy of Form 300A must be submitted **by March 2** of the year after the calendar year covered by the form. | Not a retention period, but a filing deadline. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

**How long you keep each set**

* **Tax‑related records** – keep them for **the period of limitations** that applies to each return or item (often 3–6 years, depending on the case) and at least **4 years** for employment‑tax records.  
* **OSHA injury/illness records** – keep the 300, 301, and 300A logs, plus any associated medical or exposure files, for **at least 5 years** from the date the injury or illness occurred.  
* **Other records** (e.g., payroll, asset docs, health‑safety training) are retained for the period required by the IRS or the specific regulation that applies to them.

These are the specific documents and retention periods that the provided materials require you to keep for tax purposes and for work‑related injuries.

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**Getting Your Business Off the Ground**

1. **Choose the type of business** – Decide whether you’ll operate as a sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, S‑corporation or LLC.  The type of business determines which tax return you file and how your profits and losses are reported [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=3) .

2. **Register your business name** – If you use a name that isn’t your own last name, file a fictitious‑name or assumed‑business‑name statement with the local county clerk or the Secretary of State.  Corporations and LLCs must file articles of incorporation or organization with the Secretary of State [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6) .

3. **Get a taxpayer identification number (TIN)** –  
   * If you’re a sole proprietor with no employees, you can use your Social Security number (SSN).  
   * If you have employees or you want a separate business ID, apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN).  The IRS will automatically enroll you in EFTPS when you get an EIN [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6) .

4. **Pick a tax year** –  
   * Most small businesses use a calendar year (January 1 – December 31).  
   * A fiscal year is a 12‑month period ending in a month other than December.  Choose the year you use before you file your first return; changing it later requires Form 1128 [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) .

5. **Select an accounting method** –  
   * **Cash**: record income/expense when money changes hands.  
   * **Accrual**: record income/expense when earned/occurred.  If you keep inventory, the accrual method is normally required [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) .  
   * Any change later usually needs IRS approval [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) .

6. **Open a separate business checking account** – Keep business and personal funds separate.  Use the account for all receipts and pay‑offs, and use checks (or electronic payments) that can be matched to receipts [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14) .

7. **Record every transaction** –  
   * **Daily cash receipts** and **monthly summaries** keep track of income.  
   * **Check‑disbursements journal** records all payments.  
   * Use a **business checkbook** or a computerized system that can produce legible records for the IRS [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14), [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) .

8. **Reconcile monthly** – Compare your bank statement to your ledger/checkbook; correct any discrepancies.  Do this each month so your books stay accurate [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14) .

9. **Keep supporting documents** – Retain receipts, invoices, canceled checks, account statements, and any other proof that supports the amounts in your books.  These documents are required to prove deductions and substantiate your records if the IRS reviews your return [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) .

10. **Track deductions** – Ordinary and necessary business expenses are deductible.  You can elect to deduct up to $5 000 of start‑up and organizational costs, or amortize the rest [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9) .  Keep separate records for each type of expense so you can claim them on the correct form (e.g., Schedule C for business income, Schedule E for rental income, etc.) [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) .

11. **File the proper tax forms** –  
    * **Sole proprietors**: Form 1040 with Schedule C (and Schedule SE if you owe SE tax) [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6) .  
    * **Partnerships**: Form 1065 (information return) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=3) .  
    * **Corporations**: Forms 1120 (C‑corp) or 1120‑S (S‑corp) [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6) .  
    * Employers file Forms 941/944 for payroll taxes, Form 940 for federal unemployment, etc. [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8) .  
    * Estimated tax payments are required if you expect to owe $1 000 (or $500 for a corporation) [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6) .  

12. **Pay estimated or withholding taxes on time** –  
    * Use the IRS Interactive Tax Assistant or Pub. 505 to calculate the amount.  
    * Deposit through EFTPS or FTP as required [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8) .  

13. **Keep an electronic record** – If you use an electronic storage system, it must be capable of producing a legible, complete record of all transactions and must be preserved for the same period as paper books [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12) .

---

**Quick Checklist for Keeping Taxes Organized**

- [ ] File appropriate business name/registration document  
- [ ] Obtain an EIN (and enroll in EFTPS) if needed  
- [ ] Decide on a tax year before first return  
- [ ] Choose a cash or accrual accounting method and keep it consistent  
- [ ] Open a business bank account and use it exclusively for business  
- [ ] Keep a daily record of receipts and a monthly summary of cash receipts  
- [ ] Maintain a check‑disbursements journal and reconcile monthly  
- [ ] Store all receipts, invoices, and canceled checks as supporting documents  
- [ ] Separate records for each business if you run more than one  
- [ ] File the correct tax returns and forms each year  
- [ ] Pay estimated taxes or withholdings by the due dates  
- [ ] Store electronic records in a retrievable, legible format  

Following these steps—grounded in the IRS Publication 583 and related forms—will help you start a business legally and keep your tax records in order so you can file accurately and on time.



**Sources:**

runs.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
runs.answer:
To keep your employees safe **and** make your premises fully accessible, you need to address both the physical layout of the building (walkways, doors, ramps, parking, etc.) and the operational procedures that support safe evacuation and daily use.  The handbook gives a practical checklist for each area.  Below is a concise, evidence‑based plan you can follow.

| What you need to do | Where the requirement is stated |
|----------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Make the entrance(s) accessible** – At least one public entrance must be usable by people with mobility devices. Provide a ramp or lift if stairs exist, or use an existing alternate entrance. Sign any non‑accessible entrance with a sign that directs people to the accessible one. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Ramp design** – Maximum slope 1:12, minimum width 36 in, handrail on both sides when slope > 1:20 or rise > 6 in. Provide a landing at least 18 in beyond the door, 60 in from the door horizontally. Add edge protection (lower rail or guardrail) to stop accidental rolling over the edge. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Door hardware** – Replace any door handle that requires tight grasping, twisting, or pinching with a lever handle, push plate, or loop‑type handle. If a door is less than 36 in wide, enlarge it with a “swing‑clear” hinge or remodel the frame. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Turnstiles** – Remove or replace narrow turnstiles with an accessible gate or with a wider opening (minimum 32 in). If you keep a turnstile, place an accessible gate adjacent to it. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) |
| **Accessible parking** – Provide a space for each 25 or fewer parking spaces; add a second space if the lot has 51–100 spaces. The space must have an access aisle at least 5 ft wide, 1:50 maximum slope, and a vertical clearance of 98 in. Mark the space with the international symbol and, if it is a van‑accessible space, also add the “van accessible” wording. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Walkways & work surfaces** – Keep all walkways free of holes, obstructions, or slippery patches. Cover wet surfaces with non‑slip material; place temporary mats if necessary. Provide guardrails on any elevated surface 4 ft (1.2 m) or higher. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73) |
| **Clearance for mobility devices** – Every aisle, shelf, and counter must allow a wheelchair to travel. Minimum inside width 3 ft (36 in), 30 × 48 in clearance in front of counters, 36‑in‑wide “T” turns or 60‑in. turning radius for 90‑° turns. | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Emergency action plan** – Define who can call an evacuation, what routes to use, where to assemble, and how to assist people with disabilities. Post illuminated exit signs (minimum 6 in tall, 0.75 in wide) and test emergency lighting every month (30 s) and yearly (90 min). | [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26)[[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28) |
| **Regular inspections and corrective action** – Conduct routine walk‑throughs to identify and repair hazards, keep records of inspections, and train staff on what to do if an emergency arises. | [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)[[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |
| **Workplace violence prevention** – Install physical barriers and security hardware on required exit doors, provide a written violence‑prevention plan, and train employees on de‑escalation. | [[16]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=85)[[17]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=84) |
| **Continuous improvement** – Review the plan at least annually, revise whenever your layout or staffing changes, and involve employees in hazard identification. | [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) |

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
**Writing a Business Plan**

1. **Cover Page** – Include company name, address, phone, owners, and date.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

2. **Executive Summary** – A brief two‑paragraph overview of idea, funding need, current investment, and a schedule of goals.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

3. **Business Description** – Outline product/service, competitive advantage, regulations, facilities, and equipment.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

4. **Management/Organizational Structure** – State the business form, owners, board, day‑to‑day manager, long‑term planner, and accounting responsibilities, supported with resumes.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

5. **Market Analysis** – Total market size, target segment, competition, and promotion plan.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

6. **Financial (“Money”) Section** – Include  
   - Sources & Uses of Funds statement  
   - Three‑year income projection  
   - Cash‑flow projection  
   - Break‑even analysis  
   - Supporting notes and assumptions.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

7. **Exhibits** – Resumes, purchase agreements, contracts, floor plans, etc. that substantiate the plan.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

**Setting Up Accounting**

1. **Choose a Business Entity & Get an EIN** – Sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, or LLC; obtain an Employer Identification Number if hiring or paying taxes.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

2. **Open a Separate Business Checking Account** – Keep business and personal funds separate; deposit daily receipts; write checks for all business expenses; note each deposit’s source.  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

3. **Select an Accounting Method**  
   - *Cash* (record when money is received/paid) or *Accrual* (record when earned/incurred).  
   - For inventory, generally use accrual; small businesses may treat inventory as non‑incidental.  
   - Obtain IRS approval if you change your method.  
   [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

4. **Choose a Bookkeeping System**  
   - *Single‑entry*: daily and monthly cash sums.  
   - *Double‑entry*: journals and ledgers with debits/credits that balance automatically.  
   - A computer program can be used if it produces clear, reconciliatory records.  
   [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

5. **Daily and Monthly Recordkeeping**  
   - Record each transaction in a checkbook or journal.  
   - Reconcile the checking account with bank statements each month to verify balances, bank charges, and un‑cleared items.  
   - Keep supporting documents (receipts, cancellations, invoices).  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

6. **Maintain Proper Records for Tax Filing**  
   - Keep income, expenses, assets, liabilities, and equity records to support the income statement, cash flow, and balance sheet.  
   - Retain documents per IRS guidance and to support any tax deductions (e.g., business expenses, bad debts, depreciation).  
   [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

**Key Take‑aways**

- Start the plan with a clear outline and finish the executive summary last.  
- The financial section must contain detailed projections, source/uses of funds, and break‑even analysis.  
- Keep business finances strictly separate from personal ones.  
- Reconcile bank accounts monthly, keep all receipts, and use a consistent accounting method.  
- Choose single‑ or double‑entry bookkeeping based on your comfort and business size.  
- Follow IRS rules for entity, EIN, and accounting method changes.  

These steps provide a complete, segment‑grounded approach to drafting a business plan and establishing a reliable accounting system.

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
**What you should track for taxes**

- **Business income and gross receipts** – keep receipts, sales slips, bank deposit slips, and a detailed cash‑receipts log.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
- **Deductible expenses** – record each ordinary and necessary expense.  Keep the supporting documents (invoices, receipts, canceled checks, credit‑card statements, deposit slips, etc.) that show the amount, date and business purpose.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
- **Taxes directly attributable to the business** – track the actual amounts you pay on the following and retain the proof of payment:  
  - State and local **income taxes** paid on gross income (not on federal income tax).  
  - **Employment taxes** you pay as an employer (Social Security, Medicare, FUTA, state unemployment, etc.).  
  - **Personal‑property taxes** on business‑use property (e.g., your company car).  
  - **Real‑estate taxes** on business property.  
  - **Excise taxes** you pay for fuel, heavy trucks, or other regulated business activities.  
  Records for each of these are required to substantiate the deduction on Schedule C (Form 1040).  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
- **Employment‑related deductions** – if you have employees, keep an **employment‑compensation record** (hours worked, wages, withholdings, etc.) and all payroll‑related tax records for at least 4 years.  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
- **Depreciation and asset records** – for any business property you acquire, keep purchase price, cost of improvements, acquisition date, and asset description so you can work out depreciation or basis on sale.  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

**What to track for travel expenses**

| Type of travel expense | What to record | Key points |
|------------------------|----------------|------------|
| Transportation (air, train, bus, car) | Receipts, fares, mileage/logbook entries (for car use) | Keep per‑trip receipts; for car use, record business vs. personal mileage. See the standard mileage rate (70 ¢/mile for 2025) or actual expenses. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| Taxi, commuter bus, limousines | Receipts, fare amount, purpose | Must be between a business location and a temporary workplace. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| Baggage / shipping | Shipping receipts, truck logs | For items sent between work locations. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| Car or truck operation | Logbook of business miles, mileage log, and a separate record of actual expenses (gas, oil, tires, insurance, parking, tolls, repairs) or the standard mileage rate. | Business‑use fraction determined by mileage. Must track business vs. personal miles. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| Lodging | Hotel receipts, dates of stay | Is deductible if the trip is overnight or long enough that you need rest to perform duties. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| Meals | Receipts, date, attendees, purpose | Generally 50 % deductible if the business is overnight or long‑distance trip. You may use a standard meal allowance instead of actual receipts. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| Cleaning | Receipts | For dry‑cleaning and laundry while on the trip. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| Telephone & communication | Receipts | Business‑use telephone calls made while traveling. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| Tips to service providers | Receipts | Included with related expense. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |
| Reimbursements to employees | Employee reimbursement records | Deduct the amount if paid under an accountable or non‑accountable plan. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |

**Record‑keeping rules for travel**

- Use the guidelines in **Pub. 463** – keep receipts, logs, petty‑cash slips, and any other supporting documents that demonstrate the expense and business purpose.  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
- For car/truck expenses, keep a mileage log, receipts for actual expenses (gas, oil, repairs, tires, insurance, parking, tolls), and the business‑use percentage. If you elect the standard mileage rate, you generally cannot claim actual expenses except for parking, tolls, and interest on a car loan.  
  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

**Why keeping these records matters**

- Enables you to substantiate each deduction when filing Schedule C (Form 1040) or other return forms.  
- Supports prepared tax returns and gives you a complete audit trail if the IRS reviews your return.  
- Helps you monitor expenses, prepare accurate financial statements, and comply with IRS “record retention” periods.  
  [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

**Summary**

Track **all receipts and supporting documentation** for: income, ordinary and necessary expenses, taxes you pay that are business‑directed (employment, excise, property, etc.), and every travel‑related cost (transportation, lodging, meals, tips, cleaning, phone, and car usage). Keep mileage logs



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 12)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 40)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)
3. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 13)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)
4. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)
5. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 41)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)
6. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
You **do** need an EIN (Employer Identification Number) if any of the following apply to your business:

* You pay wages to one or more employees.  
* You file pension or excise tax returns.  
* You are a partnership, LLC, corporation, or other entity that the IRS requires to use an EIN.  
* You want to use a business‑only tax identification number instead of your SSN (e.g., for a sole proprietorship with no employees).  

If you are a sole proprietor with no employees and you do not file pension or excise returns, you can use your Social Security number, but obtaining an EIN is still common and recommended for privacy and for opening a business bank account. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

---

### What accounting method do you use?

The accounting method you choose **is independent of** whether you have an EIN.  
When you file your first income‑tax return for the business, you select either a:

| Method | How you record income | How you record expenses |
|--------|----------------------|--------------------------|
| **Cash method** | Income when you receive it; expenses when you pay them. | Expense when you pay it. |
| **Accrual method** | Income when you earn it, even if payment comes later. | Expense when you incur it, even if you haven’t paid it yet. |

If your business has an inventory that you must track, you generally must use the accrual method for sales and purchases, unless you qualify as a “small business taxpayer” and can treat inventory as non‑incidental supplies. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

You decide the method when you file the tax return that first reports your business income (e.g., a Form 1040 Schedule C for a sole proprietor). If you later want to change methods, you normally need IRS approval by filing Form 3115.  

So, **an EIN does not dictate a specific accounting method; you choose the method that best fits your business when you file your first return.**  

- Need an EIN? See [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4) and [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  
- Choose an accounting method (cash or accrual, or other) when filing your first return; see [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5), [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14), [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

runs.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
runs.answer:
You should keep the OSHA injury‑and‑illness record‑keeping forms that your business is required to complete and store them for at least five years at the worksite.  

- **OSHA Form 300** – the Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses, which is filled out for each recordable injury or illness.  
- **OSHA Form 301** – the Incident Report, which supplements each recordable case.  
- **OSHA Form 300A** – the annual Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses.  

These three forms (300, 301 and 300A) must be kept at the worksite for a minimum of five years from the date of the incident or the end of the calendar year covered by the summary, whichever is later [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  

Minor injuries that only require first aid are not recordable under OSHA and therefore do not need to be filed or kept in the OSHA log [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: do i need workers comp insurance and can i deduct it
runs.answer:
You may need workers’‑comp insurance if the law in your state requires it for any employees you have.  Many states mandate workers’ comp coverage for all employers with employees, and it is a business‑expense that you can deduct on your tax return.  

**Deductibility** – Workers’ compensation premiums are listed as a deductible insurance expense for businesses.  The IRS treats these premiums as an ordinary and necessary expense that can be deducted on Schedule C (Form 1040) with the rest of your business insurance costs.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37)

**Requirement** – While the IRS does not say it is mandatory, the state‑level requirement is real.  The State Labor Department’s guidance says “To avoid civil lawsuit, it is our recommendation you carry workers’ compensation insurance for your employees.”  That statement reflects the common legal requirement in most states for employers who pay employees.  You should verify your state’s specific law, but in practice most employers are required to carry the coverage.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 37)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37)
2. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 9)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9)

runs.question: what do i file for my employees and what state taxes do i owe for them
runs.answer:
**What you must file for your employees**

| What you must file | When it’s due | Where it’s filed | Notes |
|--------------------|---------------|------------------|-------|
| **Form W‑2, Wage and Tax Statement** – reports wages, tips, other compensation, federal income tax withheld, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and any FICA matches you make | January 31 (almost always) | With each employee and the Social Security Administration (SSA) | You must also file **Form W‑3, Transmittal of Forms W‑2** to the SSA on the same date [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Employer’s quarterly payroll tax return: Form 941** – reports Social Security, Medicare, and federal income‑tax withholdings you collect and the employer’s share of Social Security and Medicare taxes | 30 April, 31 July, 31 October, 31 January (for the quarter) | Internal Revenue Service (IRS) | If doing a year‑long payroll you can use **Form 944** instead [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Federal unemployment (FUTA) return: Form 940** – reports your federal unemployment tax (paid from your own money, not withheld from workers) | 31 January (always) | IRS | Only if your liability exceeds $500 [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **State unemployment insurance return** – every state requires employers to report and pay unemployment insurance tax (the amount and due dates vary by state) | State‑specific schedule | State tax agency | Example: in South Dakota the account manager must report new hires within 20 days and pays state unemployment at the state’s schedule [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9) |
| **New‑hire reporting** – many states require a separate form or electronic filing to report every new employee within a set period after hiring | 20 calendar days after hire (example: SD) | State Department of Labor | Must submit W‑4 forms and other required information [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9) |
| **State payroll‑withholding return** (if your state has one) – reports the state income tax you withheld from employees and the amount you owe | State‑specific schedule | State tax agency | Must be filed along with the annual income‑tax return in many states [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9) |
| **Workers’ compensation insurance** – while not a federal form, employers must carry or obtain workers’ compensation coverage per state law [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9) |

**State taxes you owe on behalf of your employees**

| State tax | What you owe | Why it’s payable at the employer level |
|-----------|--------------|----------------------------------------|
| **State unemployment insurance (UI)** | A percentage of employee wages (rate set by each state) paid quarterly or annually by the employer | UI is funded by the employer’s contributions; employees pay nothing on this account |
| **State workers’ compensation insurance** | Employer‑paid premiums on each employee’s job classification | Protects employees from workplace injuries; mandated by state law |
| **State payroll tax (income‑tax withholding, if applicable)** | Amount withheld from employees’ wages (based on employee’s W‑4 or state withholding guide), then remitted to the state | Employers act as withholding agents for state income tax [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9) |
| **State excise or sales taxes** | Any applicable state excise taxes on certain business activities (e.g., fuel, tobacco, alcohol) | If you sell such products or provide taxable services, the state requires the employer to report and remit those excise taxes, usually quarterly [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8) |

**Key take‑away**

* File Form W‑2/​W‑3 for each employee; file Forms 941 (or 944) and 940 with the IRS each quarter or year.
* File the state unemployment insurance return and any required state payroll‑withholding return on the state’s schedule.
* Keep employees’ SSNs on file, have them fill out W‑4, and collect Form I‑9 for new hires.
* Pay the employer’s share of Social Security, Medicare, and FUTA taxes, and remit those with your quarterly forms.
* Pay state UI, workers’ comp, and any state payroll or excise taxes that apply to your employees or to your business activities.  

These are the federally and generally state‑level filing and tax‑paying obligations that cover employees.  

(If you operate in a specific state, check that state’s department‑of‑labor or revenue website for precise rates, due dates, and forms—State‑level requirements may differ from the examples above.)

runs.question: what if a customer cannot get through my front door and what if someone is hurt on site
runs.answer:
**What if a customer cannot get through your front door?**  
– Provide an alternative accessible entrance if it is readily achievable. A ramp, lift, or another door that meets the ADA requirements will allow the customer to enter. If a step that cannot be removed remains, you must offer an alternate service (e.g., home delivery, curb‑side pickup, or having a clerk bring the order to the customer outside). The alternative must be publicized so the customer knows how to obtain the goods or services [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  
– If the accessible entrance is a separate door, sign the location clearly and keep it open during business hours. If you must lock it for security, install an accessible call box or buzzer that a customer can use to request staff to unlock it; the call system must be mounted at an accessible height (generally ≤48 in.) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18).  
– When you use an alternate entrance or service, make sure the route to the entrance is clear, at least 36 in. wide, and that any aisle or passage is marked with appropriate signage (e.g., international symbol of accessibility). If a turnstile or other barrier exists, remove it or replace it with an accessible gate if readily achievable. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

runs.question: how much cash before i have to report it and do i need a licence to serve food
runs.answer:
You only have to file a special reporting form when a **single cash transaction (or two or more related transactions) exceeds $10,000**. That filing is called Form 8300, “Report of Cash Payments Over $10,000 Received in a Trade or Business.” The rule treats cash as U.S. and foreign coin and currency, as well as cashier’s or traveler’s checks and money orders; it does **not** include a personal check. If you take more than $10,000 in a single transaction you must file Form 8300; otherwise you’re not required to file that form. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)

To serve food you **must** have a food license from the local health department. Before a food license (or a lodging license) is issued, you must first complete an inspection and obtain approval from the Department of Health. This applies to any business that prepares and serves food. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=8)

runs.question: how do i register a trademark
runs.answer:
A trademark gives you the exclusive right to use a name, logo, sound, or other mark that identifies your goods or services. To register one you can choose either a **state‑level** or a **federal‑level** filing.  

1. **Decide which level of protection you want.**  
   * State registration protects the mark only within that state.  
   * Federal registration (through the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, USPTO) protects the mark nationwide and opens up federal court rights.  

2. **Search existing marks.**  
   * Before filing you should search the trademark databases (both state and USPTO) to confirm that no identical or confusingly similar mark is already registered or pending.

3. **File the application.**  
   * At the state level you file with the Secretary of State’s office.  
   * At the federal level you file with the USPTO, usually via the TEAS online system.

4. **After filing, the registration gives you exclusive right to use the mark** for the goods or services listed in the application.

**Contacts for filing or inquiries**

* Secretary of State (state‑level) – (605) 773‑2797 – https://sdsos.gov/ [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)  
* U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (federal‑level) – (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199 – www.uspto.gov [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
You must keep tax records for the length of time that the IRS could still need them. In practice that means:

* Keep the records that support an item of income or deduction on a tax return until the **period of limitations** for that return expires. For most personal income‑tax returns, that period is the time it takes the IRS to assess additional tax – usually **3 years** after the return was filed.  
* For employment taxes (pay‑roll, FUTA, etc.) keep all employment‑tax records for at least **4 years** after the date the tax became due or was paid, whichever is later.  
* For property (assets) you must keep records relating to the property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of that property in a taxable disposition. These records are needed to calculate depreciation, amortization, or the gain/loss on a sale.  
* Keep copies of your filed tax returns, because they are useful for preparing future returns and for showing your records if you ever file an amended return.  

These rules apply broadly and are the guidance the IRS gives on how long to keep your business and personal tax records [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records because they serve several essential purposes for your business and for compliance with federal tax law:

1. **Show that you are keeping a proper accounting system.**  
   All businesses must have an accounting method that clearly shows income and expenses for the tax year. The records you keep are the proof that you are following that method.   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

2. **Monitor the performance of your business.**  
   Good records let you see which products or services are selling, whether the business is improving, and what changes you might need to make.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  

3. **Prepare accurate financial statements.**  
   Income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets are made from the records you keep.  These statements are useful for dealing with banks, creditors, and for internal decision‑making.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  

4. **Support the information you report on your tax return.**  
   The IRS requires that you keep supporting documents (sales slips, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, etc.) that back up the amounts you report on your return.  If the IRS examines your return, having a complete set of records speeds up the review.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

5. **Meet legal and regulatory deadlines.**  
   You must keep certain records for a prescribed number of years (e.g., up to 7 years for most income‑tax items; at least 4 years for employment‑tax records).  These records are needed to complete amended returns, defend against assessments, or answer IRS questions.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

6. **Support other reporting obligations.**  
   Records are also needed for other required filings (information returns like Forms W‑2, 1099, Form 941 for employment taxes, etc.).  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  

In short, keeping detailed, organized business records lets you track how your business is doing, allows you to file accurate tax returns and other required reports, complies with the IRS’s retention rules, and protects you in case of an audit.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
**Choosing an Accounting Method**

When you first file an income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for your business, you select an accounting method.  That method must be used for all future tax returns unless you obtain IRS approval to change it.

|   | What to consider | Typical choice | IRS rule |
|---|------------------|----------------|----------|
| **1. Inventory** | Does your business keep inventory of goods you sell? | **Accrual** if you have inventory, unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer and elect to treat inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies. | “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method …” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **2. Size of business** | Average annual gross receipts ≤ $31 million for the last 3 years (inflation‑adjusted) and not a tax shelter. | Small‑business taxpayers may use the cash method even with inventory, provided inventory is treated as non‑incidental materials or conforms to your financial accounting. | “You qualify as a small business taxpayer if...” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **3. Type of business** | Sole proprietor, partnership, or S‑corporation | No special rule on method; choose based on inventory and size. | “You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return that includes a Schedule C” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **4. Simplicity vs. matching** | Cash method: report income when received, expenses when paid.  Accrual method: match income earned with expenses incurred. | Cash method is easier for simple, cash‑based businesses.  Accrual method gives a clearer picture of the business’s financial position. | “Under the cash method, you report income in the tax year you receive it” and “Under the accrual method, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |
| **5. Changing methods later** | If you later decide the current method is not suitable, you must file Form 3115 for a change of accounting method and may need IRS approval or a user fee. | “Once you have set up your accounting method, you must generally get IRS approval before you can change to another method” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) |

### Quick decision cheat sheet

1. **No inventory** → Use the **cash method** (unless you have a specific reason to choose accrual).  
2. **Inventory**  
   - Small‑business taxpayer treating inventory as non‑incidental supplies → cash method possible.  
   - Otherwise → **accrual method**.  
3. **Combination**: You may use a combination of cash, accrual, or special methods for different items, but the overall method must consistently show your income.  If you mix methods, the combination is treated as cash method if any cash method is used. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

### When you change it

- File **Form 3115** to get approval or rely on the automatic change procedures.  
- A user fee may apply unless you qualify for automatic approval. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)

**Bottom line:** Pick the method that matches your business activities.  For most sole‑prophetors with no inventory, the **cash method** is simplest and most common.  If you hold inventory, use the **accrual method**, unless you are a qualified small‑business taxpayer and choose to treat inventory as non‑incidental supplies.  Keep consistent records and consult Form 3115 if you later decide to change.

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
**How to Check Your Workplace for Hazards**

1. **Use a Self‑Inspection Checklist**  
   * Start with the self‑inspection checklists in the handbook. They cover general industry hazards (not construction or maritime) and show where to begin fixing problems.  
   * The checklists are based on OSHA standards and accepted safety principles, but the handbook reminds you that they are **not a substitute for a compliance assessment** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).

2. **Gather Supporting Information**  
   * Combine the completed checklist data with injury and illness logs, training records, maintenance logs, and incident reports. This helps you spot patterns and prioritize fixes [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).

3. **Involve Your Workers**  
   * Schedule inspections with regular staff, ask for hazard ideas, and let workers help decide on and test controls. The handbook lists this as a core element of a safety program [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9).

4. **Document the Inspection**  
   * Record the date, who inspected, the location, and any hazards found. A simple table template is in the handbook (Company name, Worksite, Specific area, Inspected by, Date) – use it for consistency [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9).

5. **Control and Verify Hazards**  
   * Once a hazard is identified, implement engineering, administrative, or protective‑equipment controls. Follow up with a post‑control check to make sure the measure works and stays effective [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7).

6. **Repeat Regularly**  
   * The handbook stresses routine inspections, not one‑off reviews. A “routine” inspection could be monthly, quarterly, or as often as your industry requires—adjust the frequency to match your risk level [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7).

7. **Use OSHA Resources for Help**  
   * For detailed guidance, OSHA’s Online Training and consultation programs are available. The handbook notes that the On‑Site Consultation program offers free, confidential help for small businesses [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90).

**Quick Recap**  
- **Prepare** a checklist (based on OSHA standards).  
- **Insist** on a regular, team‑based inspection.  
- **Record** findings clearly.  
- **Control** hazards and **verify** the fix.  
- **Repeat** to keep hazards at bay.

These steps are the exact procedure the handbook recommends for checking a workplace for hazards.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash vs. accrual accounting are two different ways to record a business’s income and expenses for tax purposes:

**Cash method**  
- You count income only when you actually receive the money (or when it is constructively received).  
- You deduct or capitalize expenses only in the year you pay them.  
- Example: you got a $500 check on December 30 2025 but couldn’t deposit it until January 3 2026; you must report that $500 as income for 2025, not 2026, because the check was received in 2025 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).

**Accrual method**  
- You record income in the year it is earned, regardless of when the cash is received.  
- You deduct or capitalize expenses in the year the expense is incurred, even if the payment is made later.  
- Purpose: to match income with the expenses that created it.  
- Example: you sold a computer on December 28 2025, got billed in January 2026, and received payment in February 2026; you must include the revenue in 2025 income because the computer was sold in that year [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=29).

**Key points that distinguish the two**

| Feature | Cash method | Accrual method |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| Income reported | When received (or constructively received) | When earned (all‑events test met) |
| Expense reported | When paid | When incurred (all‑events test met, economic performance done) |
| Inventory requirement | Not required unless you keep inventory, but if you do you still need accrual for purchases/sales | Required to use accrual for inventory purchases and sales unless you are a small‑business taxpayer that elects otherwise |

When you first file a tax return you choose one method; you must keep the same method consistent across all income calculations and bookkeeping [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

In short, cash accounting matches the timing of money flowing in and out, while accrual accounting matches the timing of when economic activities (sales, services, purchases) occur, irrespective of when cash actually changes hands.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 29)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=29)
