runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes, you can deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that you incur while traveling for business.  
The IRS allows you to deduct the following travel‑related costs, as long as the trip meets the basic “away‑from‑home” test (you must be away from the general area of your tax home for longer than an ordinary day’s work and need sleep or rest to perform your duties) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).  

| Item you can deduct | How it works | Key limits or rules |
|---------------------|--------------|---------------------|
| **Travel by air, train, bus, or car** | Deduct the actual cost of transportation between your home and a business destination, or between a business destination and a hotel, etc. | The expense must be ordinary and necessary. |
| **Taxis, commuter buses, limousines, rideshares** | Deduct fares for travel between airports, stations, hotels, and work locations away from home. | Same ordinary‑and‑necessary rule applies. |
| **Baggage, shipping, and freight** | Deduct costs for sending baggage, samples, or display material between your regular and temporary work locations. | Must be business‑related. |
| **Car or truck use while traveling away from home** | You may deduct either actual operating costs (fuel, oil, tires, insurance, depreciation, lease payments, etc.) or the standard mileage rate (currently 70 ¢/mile for 2025, 75 ¢/mile for 2026) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35). If you use the standard rate, you can still deduct parking fees and tolls. | If you use the standard rate in the first year a vehicle becomes available, you cannot switch to actual expenses later that same year unless you use a different vehicle. |
| **Meals and lodging** | You may deduct the cost of meals and hotel lodging on an overnight or long‑duration business trip. You can choose the actual costs or a standard meal allowance. For 2025 the deduction for meals is 50 % of the cost (unless you qualify for a 100 % deduction for certain circumstances such as health‑care workers). Lodging is 100 % deductible. | Use Pub. 463 for detailed limits and record‑keeping. |
| **Other incidental expenses** | You may deduct dry‑cleaning, laundry, telephone calls made on the trip, tips paid on any expense item in this list, and other incidental costs that are ordinary and necessary. | All must be directly related to the business purpose of the trip. |

**Key points to remember**

* The deduction applies only to the **business‑use portion** of expenses if you use the vehicle or lodging partially for personal reasons.  
* The trip must qualify as a "business trip," meaning you’re required to be away from the general area of your tax home and you need rest to perform your duties while away [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).  
* Keep accurate records (mileage logs, receipts, dates, business purpose) because you must be able to show that the expense was ordinary, necessary, and closely tied to your business [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  
* For meals, you cannot deduct 100 % of the cost except for specific professions (e.g., health‑care workers) [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).

So, if you pay for a car, flights, lodging, meals, or other transportation costs while traveling out of town for your business, those expenses are generally deductible on Schedule C (Form 1040) [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).



**Sources:**

runs.question: what goes in an executive summary
runs.answer:
An executive summary should be a concise overview—normally one to two paragraphs—of the key points of your business plan. It gives the reader a quick sense of what you want to accomplish, including:

* The core business idea or product/service you are offering.  
* How much funding you require, what the money will be used for, and how much capital you have already invested.  
* A brief outline of your financial projections or funding plan.  
* A short schedule of your major milestones or goals.  

Because it is written last, it reflects the full detail of the plan while remaining brief enough to capture the reader’s attention.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To describe your target market, follow the guidance in the business‑planning guide:

1. **Define the niche** – Identify the specific group of customers who are most likely to buy your product or service.  Explain why this group is the best fit for what you offer.  In particular, describe their key characteristics such as age, gender, income, lifestyle, or the particular problem your product solves.  Use terms like “market niche” and “best customer” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14).

2. **Segment the market** – For B2B markets, classify customers by industry, company size, location, or how they will use the product.  For consumer markets, segment by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14).

3. **Estimate size and growth** – Use population data, sales tax information, industry reports, or other statistics to approximate the total number of potential customers in each segment.  Project the growth potential of those segments and estimate how much of the total market you can realistically capture.  This provides a quantitative basis for your target market description [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14).

4. **Provide examples** – Illustrate with concrete examples of a typical customer in each segment so that readers can visualize who you are targeting.  This makes the description more vivid and actionable.

By combining these steps, you create a clear, data‑driven portrait of the target market that can guide your marketing, pricing, and product‑development decisions.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
**Short answer:**  
Yes.  If your shop is a private business that serves the public, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires you to make the shop accessible to people who use wheelchairs (or other mobility aids) *if it is “readily achievable.”*  That means you must remove or mitigate architectural barriers that can be fixed without extraordinary expense or difficulty, and you must provide the accessibility features that the ADA standards specify.

---

## What “readily achievable” means

* “Readily achievable” is defined as something that can be accomplished “easily accomplishable without much difficulty or expense” and is determined by the size and resources of the business【Segment 10】.  Larger businesses can be expected to act more aggressively than very small shops, but *any* business that saw the public must look for barriers that can be removed.

---

## Key components you need to address

| Feature | ADA requirement (if favorable) | Source |
|---------|--------------------------------|--------|
| **Accessible entrance** | At least one entrance must be accessible.  If there’s any other entrance that is accessible, a sign must direct people to it; the alternative entrance must remain open during business hours.  A ramp must have a slope no steeper than 1:12 and hand‑rails when the rise is >6 in. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Door hardware** | All door handles must be operable without a tight grasp, twist, or pinching.  Replace knobs with lever handles or use a “loop‑type” handle. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Accessible parking** | Provide at least one accessible parking space if 25 or fewer total spaces, two if 50 or fewer (and at least one of those must be van‑accessible).  The space must be 5 ft wide, have a 5‑ft access aisle, 98‑in. vertical clearance, and be located on level ground or with a curb ramp. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) |
| **Accessible route inside** | A continuous wheelchair‑accessible path that is at least 36 in. wide, no steep slopes, no steps, and clear of obstacles.  A 3‑ft‑by‑3‑ft turning space is required at corners, and a 60‑in. diameter turning space if a 180° turn is needed. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Sales/service counter** | One counter section at least 36 in. long and no higher than 36 in. above the floor, with 30 in. × 48 in. clear floor space in front so the person can approach.  An auxiliary counter or folding shelf may satisfy the requirement if the main counter can’t be modified. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Tables & seating (if applicable)** | If your shop has fixed tables, at least 5 % (or at least one if fewer than 20) must be accessible.  A table’s surface must be 28–34 in. high with 27 in. knee clearance and a 30 in. × 48 in. clear floor area. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) |
| **Signage** | All accessible routes must have signs with the international symbol of accessibility, located high enough to be seen. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Policy changes** | Adjust any policies that artificially restrict access – e.g., lockable “accessible” doors, exclude service animals, or limit where accessible customers can sit. Provide an accessible call bell if a door remains locked for security. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18) |

---

## When you’re exempt

* If your shop was built before **January 26, 1993** and has not been altered **after January 26, 1992**, the ADA allows a *less strict* set of requirements for “existing facilities.”  Even so, barriers that are “readily achievable” must be removed.  That generally means eliminating narrow aisles, steps at entry, or unreachable counters if possible. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6) |

---

## How to proceed

1. **Walk‑through audit** – Use the list above to identify any barriers.  If a barrier needs modifications that are clearly *readily achievable* (e.g., widen a doorway, install a ramp, provide a low counter section), do it.
2. **Documentation** – Keep a record of the barriers you identified and the actions you took.  This can help you defend yourself if a complaint is filed.
3. **Consider cost‑sharing incentives** – If the modifications cost more than you can afford, you might qualify for a tax credit (up to $5,000) or a deduction (up to $15,000) for barrier‑removal expenses【Segment 17】.
4. **Stay current** – If you later renovate or add new areas, the new spaces must comply with the ADA standards from the date of their opening【Segment 13】.

---

### Bottom line

Because a shop that serves the public falls under the ADA’s definition of a *public accommodation*, **you are required to make your shop wheelchair‑accessible if the required changes are readily achievable**.

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
You may be exempt from OSHA’s injury‑and‑illness record‑keeping requirements only under two conditions, and you must still report certain severe incidents even if exempt.

* **Small‑worker exemption** – If your business had **10 or fewer employees during the entire previous calendar year**, you are partially exempt from keeping OSHA Form 300 (the injury log), Form 301 (incident reports), and Form 300A (annual summary).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

* **Low‑hazard exemption** – If your industry is listed as “low‑hazard” in **29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A**, you also qualify for the same partial exemption.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

Even with either exemption, you **must** report:

* Work‑related **fatalities**,
* **In‑patient hospitalizations**,
* **Amputations**, and
* **Loss of an eye**,

within the required time frames (within 8 hours for deaths, within 24 hours for the others).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

If your business does **not** meet either exemption criterion, you are required to keep the full OSHA injury records and submit the summaries electronically when applicable.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

This retention period applies to all workers who are required to keep OSHA injury records, whether the records are kept on paper or electronically [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**

1. **Choose a legal structure**  
   - Decide whether you’ll be a sole‑prop, partnership, LLC, or corporation. The structure determines the tax return you file and the taxes you owe.  
   - For a sole‑prop or partnership you’ll use Schedule C or 1065; for a corporation use Form 1120 (C) or 1120‑S (S).  
   - Refer to the “Legal and tax considerations” section of the publication for details. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=3)  

2. **Get a taxpayer identification number (TIN)**  
   - Most businesses need an Employer Identification Number (EIN). Individuals who don’t have employees can also choose an EIN to keep business and personal taxes separate.  
   - Apply online at IRS.gov or submit Form SS‑4. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  

3. **Pick a tax year**  
   - You may use a calendar year (Jan 1 – Dec 31) or a fiscal year ending on any month except December.  
   - If you file your first return with a calendar year, you must keep that year unless you obtain IRS approval (Form 1128). [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

4. **Choose an accounting method**  
   - **Cash method**: record income when received and expenses when paid.  
   - **Accrual method**: record income and expenses when earned/incurred, regardless of cash flow.  
   - Changes in method usually require IRS approval (Pub. 538). [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

5. **Set up a record‑keeping system**  
   - Keep a separate business checking account and a business checkbook. Record every transaction immediately, noting the source of the receipt.  
   - Maintain supporting documents (receipts, invoices, sales slips, deposit slips, canceled checks).  
   - Store records electronically or on paper, but you must keep them in a retrievable form and preserve them for the period of limitations. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

6. **Track deductible expenses**  
   - Ordinary and necessary business expenses are deductible. Examples are office supplies, advertising, travel, vehicle costs, and start‑up costs (up to $5,000 if under $50,000).  
   - Start‑up and organizational costs above the deduction limit must be amortized over 15 years (Form 4562). [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)  

7. **Pay taxes on time**  
   - Most self‑employed taxpayers must make **estimated tax payments** when income meets the $1,000 (or $500 for corporations) threshold. Use Form 1040‑ES.  
   - File employment taxes quarterly (Form 941) if you hire employees; annually (Form 944) if your payroll is <$<PhoneNumber>.  
   - Depict corporate income taxes with Form 1120‑W if required.  
   - Follow the deadline calendar in Pub. 509 (tax calendars). [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)[[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=47)  

8. **File the correct forms**  
   - Schedule C (Form 1040) for sole‑prop income and expenses.  
   - Schedule SE (Form 1040) for self‑employment tax if net earnings ≥$400.  
   - 1065 for partnerships, 1120 for C‑corp, 1120‑S for S‑corp.  
   - Information returns: 1099‑MISC, 1099‑NEC, 1099‑B, 1099‑K if applicable.  
   - Use the appropriate schedule for each business you run. [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=3)[[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

9. **Keep records for the correct length of time**  
   - Income and deduction records: keep until the tax‑year limitations period ends (usually 3–4 years).  
   - Employment tax records: keep at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or was paid.  
   - Asset records (depreciation, basis) until you sell the asset and the tax‑year limitations expire.  
   - Preserve records longer if required by other laws (e.g., insurance, creditors). [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

10. **Monitor and adjust**

runs.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
runs.answer:
To keep your employees safe and make your premises accessible you need to follow a set of specific, documented actions that are described in the handbook.  The key requirements are:

1. **Establish a safety‑and‑health program**  
   • A written program that identifies hazards, provides training, and is reviewed annually.  
   • Workers are trained to identify and report hazards, to use PPE, and to follow evacuation procedures.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

2. **Keep walkways and working surfaces safe**  
   • Walk‑working surfaces must be kept clean, free of obstructions, and marked with non‑slip material if wet.  
   • Holes, spills, and equipment that could block walkways must be repaired or removed immediately.  
   • Aisles that run near moving machinery must provide safe clearance and guardrails if the space is more than 4 ft (1.2 m) high.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)

3. **Provide and maintain accessible entrances**  
   • At least one entrance must be accessible, or a second entrance can be used if the first is not.  
   • If an alternative entrance is used, a sign must direct customers to it, and a call box or buzzer (at most 48 in above the floor) must be on an accessible route.  
   • Ramps must have a slope no steeper than 1:12, handrails where slope > 1:20 or rise > 6 in, and edge protection.  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

4. **Make doors and door hardware accessible**  
   • Doors should be at least 36 in wide (32 in clear width when opened) and use lever or loop handles that require no tight grasping.  
   • Revolving or narrow turnstiles must have an accessible gate or opening.  
   [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)

5. **Provide accessible parking and routes to the building**  
   • Each accessible car space must have a 5‑ft wide access aisle; van spaces need an 8‑ft wide aisle.  
   • Parking spaces should be adjacent to an accessed entrance and on a level surface (max 1:50 slope).  
   • Mark spaces with the international symbol of accessibility and, for van spaces, add “van accessible.”  
   [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)

6. **Secure access to elevated areas**  
   • Guardrails, safety nets, or personal fall protection must be provided on surfaces over 4 ft high.  
   • Toeboards or screens should be installed to keep objects from falling.  
   [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73)

7. **Maintain ladders and other climbing equipment in good condition**  
   • Ladders must be inspected, served, have non‑conductive side rails if they could contact live wires, and be secured to prevent slipping.  
   • The top of portable ladders used to reach an elevated surface must extend at least 3 ft above that surface.  
   [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=75)

8. **Implement an emergency action plan**  
   • The plan must identify evacuation routes, a chain of command, key personnel contacts, and procedures for assisting people with disabilities.  
   • Emergency plan requirements are reviewed annually and updated as needed.  
   [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=25)

9. **Prepare for heat‑related illness if you work in hot conditions**  
   • Assign a trained individual to monitor temperature and humidity, implement a heat plan, and provide shade, fluids, and rest breaks.  
   • A buddy system and emergency contact instructions should be in place.  
   [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=43)

10. **Address special hazards** (e.g., electrical, machinery) as required by the specific industry; lockout/tag‑out, grounding, and signage help keep workers safe.  
    [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=18)

Following these elements ensures that your workplace protects employees from physical hazards, provides appropriate training, and remains fully accessible to people with disabilities.

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
**What you should keep track of for taxes**

1. **Gross receipts and income** – keep documents that show the source and amount of every payment you receive: cash register tapes, bank deposit slips, receipts books, invoices, 1099‑MISC and 1099‑NEC forms, etc. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
2. **Business expenses** – record every ordinary and necessary cost that your business incurs. Use supporting documents such as canceled checks, credit‑card slips, invoices, and petty‑cash slips for small payments. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
3. **Tax‑specific deductions**  
   * **State and local taxes** – record state or local income taxes that apply directly to your business and any real‑estate, personal‑property, or sales tax you pay on business items. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
   * **Employment taxes** – keep records of the social‑security, Medicare, FUTA, and unemployment taxes you pay as an employer. These must be kept for at least four years after the tax becomes due or is paid. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
   * **Depreciation and extraordinary expenditures** – keep purchase invoices, sales invoices, and dates of acquisition and disposal for assets to compute depreciation (e.g., using MACRS). [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=17)  
4. **Petty‑cash and small‑payment recordkeeping** – every petty‑cash transaction should have a petty‑cash slip and attachment that shows the receipt. The total of slips should equal the fixed amount of the fund. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

**What you should keep track of for travel expenses**

1. **Travel‑related transportation** – keep receipts or logs for air, train, bus, or car travel between your home and a business destination, and for taxi, commuter‑bus, or limousine fare between the airport/rail‑station and a hotel, or between a hotel and the work site. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
2. **Baggage and shipping** – keep receipts for sending baggage or display material between regular and temporary work locations. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
3. **Rental and parking** – keep receipts for car or truck rental, parking fees, and tolls incurred while traveling away from home. If you elect the standard mileage rate, you can still deduct parking fees and tolls. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
4. **Meals and lodging** – for overnight or long‑duration trips where you must sleep or rest, you may deduct 50 % of the cost of meals and 100 % of lodging. Keep the actual receipts; you may also use the standard meal allowance. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
5. **Telephone and communication** – keep records of calls or fax machines used while traveling. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
6. **Travel logs** – keep a detailed log of travel dates, purpose, and business mileage when you’re using a personal vehicle for business trips. If you use the standard mileage rate, keep a log of business miles to substantiate the deduction. The standard mileage rate for 2025 is 70 ¢ per mile. [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)  
7. **Reimbursement records** – if employees are reimbursed, keep the reimbursement record and note whether it is under an accountable or non‑accountable plan. The reimbursement may affect what you need to report on the employee’s W‑2. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  

**Record‑keeping notes**

* Support all expense entries with receipts, invoices, canceled checks, or electronic statements that show the amount, payee, and date. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
* Keep all records for the period required by the statute of limitations: generally until the period of limitations for the return runs out, and for employment tax records at least four years. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

These are the items you should specifically track to support your tax filings and claim for deductible travel expenses.

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
**Answer**

Yes, you usually need an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if you do one of the following:

* Pay wages to one or more employees.  
* File pension or excise tax returns.  
* Use the EIN as a tax‑payer identification number (TIN) on your business forms (for example, on Schedule C for a sole‑prop‑or‑ty) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).

If you are a sole proprietor who has no employees and you are happy to use your Social Security number (SSN) as your TIN, you are **not** required to get an EIN. However, getting an EIN can still be useful for separating personal and business finances or for businesses that might hire employees in the future [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).

---

### What accounting method do you use?

The EIN itself does **not** determine which accounting method you must use.  
When you file your first income‑tax return you choose an accounting method, and you must keep that method consistently unless you obtain IRS approval to change it.

* **Cash method** – Record income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them. This is common for many sole proprietors who do not keep inventory [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).
* **Accrual method** – Record income in the year you earn it and expenses in the year you incur them. You are required to use this method if your business must keep inventory (e.g., a retail shop) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

Other special or combination methods exist, but the choice between cash and accrual is made independently of whether you have an EIN [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

**Summary**

* Obtain an EIN if you pay employees or file pension/excise tax returns; otherwise you can use your SSN.  
* The accounting method (cash or accrual, or a special/combination method) is chosen separately when you file your first return and is not tied to having an EIN.  
* If you keep inventory, you must use an accrual method; otherwise you can typically use the cash method [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

runs.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
runs.answer:
You must keep OSHA injury and illness records:

* **OSHA Form 300** – the Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses.  
* **OSHA Form 301** – the Injury and Illness Incident Report.  
* **OSHA Form 300A** – the annual Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses.  

Retention: keep the Form 300, Form 301, and Form 300A records at the worksite for **at least five years** after the end of the calendar year in which an injury or illness occurred.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: do i need workers comp insurance and can i deduct it
runs.answer:
You do need workers’‑compensation insurance if you have employees, because it is required by state law and is treated as a regular business expense. The premiums you pay for it can be deducted from your business income on Schedule C (Form 1040) as an ordinary and necessary expense. 

- Workers’‑comp insurance is “set by state law that covers any claims for bodily injuries or job‑related diseases suffered by employees in your business, regardless of fault” and may be deducted as an insurance premium. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37)  
- The state of South Dakota, for example, explicitly recommends that employers carry workers’‑comp to avoid civil lawsuits. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9)

runs.question: what do i file for my employees and what state taxes do i owe for them
runs.answer:
**What you must file for your employees (federal forms)**  
- **Form W‑2, Wage and Tax Statement** – give a copy to each employee who earned wages during the year and file a copy with the Social Security Administration by January 31. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)  
- **Form W‑3, Transmittal of Wage and Tax Statements** – file with the SSA as a combined report of all W‑2s you filed. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)  
- **Form 941, Employer’s QUARTERLY Federal Tax Return** (or **Form 944, Employer’s ANNUAL Federal Tax Return** if you qualify) – report and pay the employer’s share of Social Security, Medicare, and federal income tax withheld for each quarter. Due dates: April 30, July 31, October 31, and January 31 each year. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)  
- **Form 940, Employer’s Annual Federal Unemployment (FUTA) Tax Return** – report and pay the annual FUTA tax. It is filed every year, typically by January 31. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)  
- **Form I‑9, Employment Eligibility Verification** – each new employee must fill this out upon hire, and you must keep it on file. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)  
- **Form W‑4, Employee’s Withholding Certificate** – each employee completes this form so you know how much federal income tax to withhold. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)  

**What to collect from employees**  
- Social Security number (SSN) for each employee.  
- Complete Form W‑4 for withholding.  
- Completed Form I‑9 to verify work eligibility. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7)

---

**State‑level payroll taxes**

The specific state payroll tax obligations depend on the state in which you employ workers.  
A common requirement exists in many states to contribute to the state’s unemployment insurance program. For example, in South Dakota you must:

- Make quarterly contributions to the state unemployment insurance fund.  
- Contact the State Department of Labor for instructions, and file reports as required. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9)

Other states impose state income‑tax withholding and other payroll taxes that must be reported on the appropriate state return or payroll‑tax forms. While the segments above focus on federal forms and give an example for South Dakota, you should consult the tax agency in each state where you have employees to determine the exact forms, due dates, and rates for state unemployment, income‑tax withholding, and any other payroll taxes. ▻︎

> If the question about “state taxes you owe for them” applies to a state other than South Dakota, the provided segments do not contain that state’s specific forms or rates, so you will need to review the relevant state’s tax agency guidance.

runs.question: what if a customer cannot get through my front door and what if someone is hurt on site
runs.answer:
**1. Customer can’t get through the front door**

- **Make the entrance physically accessible** – If the door is too narrow (less than 36 in. clear width) or its hardware prevents easy opening, you should enlarge the opening or replace the hardware with a lever‑type handle or a clamp‑on lever. A null‑grasp, thumb‑latch‑free handle will open the door without the need to grip tightly. These modifications are inexpensive and “readily achievable” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12).  
- **Keep exit doors unlocked and unobstructed** – Exit doors that serve as the primary entrance must not be locked, blocked, or otherwise obstructed and must open “from the direction of exit travel without the use of a key, tool, or any special knowledge or effort when the building is occupied” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=23).  
- **Provide an alternative accessible entrance** – If the main doorway can’t be made accessible, you must supply a second access that meets the same accessibility standards. Signage must be installed to direct customers to the alternative entrance, and the sign must be mounted at an accessible height (generally not more than 48 in. above the ground) [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
- **Keep the alternative entrance unlocked during business hours** – If security concerns prevent leaving the door unlocked, install an accessible call box or buzzer (sign‑posted and mounted at an accessible height) so that a person with a disability can request staff to unlock the door [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18).  
- **Add ramps or other ways to eliminate a step** – If a single step at the entrance blocks access, you can add a ramp with a slope no steeper than 1:12, handrails, and a wide landing (minimum 18 in. beyond the door, 60 in. in front) to provide a smooth, level approach. If the ramp can’t be built, home or curb‑side delivery may be required as an alternative service [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).  

**2. Someone is hurt on site**

- **Have a first‑aid kit and trained staff** – At least one worker on each shift must be adequately trained and qualified to render first aid, and fully supplied first‑aid kits must be easily accessible in each work area and periodically inspected and replenished [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=62). If a medical facility is near the workplace, it should be identified as the nearest point of care; otherwise, staff must know how to contact emergency services.  
- **Record and report the injury** – For injuries that are not minor first‑aid cases, fill out OSHA Form 301 (Injury/Illness Incident Report) and log it on OSHA Form 300. All work‑related fatalities must be reported to OSHA within 8 hours, and hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye within 24 hours [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).  
- **Use an Emergency Action Plan** – The plan should identify chain‑of‑command, evacuation conditions, procedures for assisting people with disabilities, and assembly points. It also describes how visitors and workers are alerted (including disabled workers) and includes a method for accounting for all personnel after an emergency [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26).  
- **Maintain a safe workplace to prevent future injuries** – Remove hazardous conditions, keep walk‑working surfaces clear, and ensure adequate barriers on street‑level exits to protect occupants from vehicular traffic [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79).  

By following the doorway modifications and emergency‑response procedures outlined above, you can make your business physically accessible to all customers and respond properly when someone is hurt on site.

runs.question: how much cash before i have to report it and do i need a licence to serve food
runs.answer:
**Answer**

**Cash reporting threshold**  
If your business receives more than **$10,000 in cash in a single transaction or in two or more related transactions, you must file Form 8300, “Report of Cash Payments Over $10,000 Received in a Trade or Business.”** This requirement applies regardless of whether the cash is paid in coins, bills, or in other monetary instruments such as cashier’s or traveler’s checks. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  

**License to serve food**  
To prepare and serve food you need a food‑service license (often called a “food establishment” or “restaurant” permit). **Approval from the state Department of Health is required before a food license or lodging license can be issued.** Other permits may be needed depending on local regulations (liquor, beer, wine, or specialized food‑service permits), but the basic requirement is the health department approval and the associated license. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=8)  

**In short:**  

- Report cash payments over $10,000 with Form 8300.  
- Obtain a food‑service license from the Department of Health (and any other local permits that apply).

runs.question: why should i bother with a safety program and what records do i need to keep
runs.answer:
**Why a safety program is worth the effort**  
A safety and health program is not just a box‑check; it protects workers, keeps your business compliant, and saves money.  The handbook explains that small employers can keep their operations “sound, productive, and profitable” if they:
- Prevent injuries and illnesses, which otherwise cost more in premiums, medical bills, and training replacement workers.  
- Improve compliance with laws, reducing the risk of inspections and penalties.  
- Reduce workers‑compensation costs and improve worker morale.  
- Engage workers, making safety a part of everyday work.  
- Enhance social‑responsibility goals and overall business operations.   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6)  

**What records you must keep**  
| Record | What it covers | Where it is kept | Retention period | Reporting requirement |
|--------|----------------|------------------|------------------|-----------------------|
| **OSHA Form 300 — Log of Work‑Related Injuries & Illnesses** | Every recordable injury/illness (excluding minor first‑aid cases) | At the worksite | 5 years |  |
| **OSHA Form 301 — Injury & Illness Incident Report** | Detailed incident data for each recordable case | At the worksite | 5 years |  |
| **OSHA Form 300A — Summary of Work‑Related Injuries & Illnesses** | Annual summary of the year’s incidents | At the worksite; electronically submitted if required | 5 years | Submit electronically by **March 2** of the year after the calendar year covered *if* you have 250 + workers or 20‑249 workers in certain high‑hazard industries, or 100 + workers in high‑hazard industries.   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** | Clinical or exposure data required by 29 CFR 1910.1020 | At the worksite | As long as the specific regulation requires it (often the same period as the injury record) |  |
| **Worker training records** | Documentation that employees received required safety training | On‑site and accessible for review | At least as long as training is required; often 5 years |  |
| **Fatality or severe‑injury reports** | Any work‑related fatality, hospital admission, amputation, or loss of an eye | Reported to OSHA within the time limits |  |
| | |  |  | **Fatalities** – within **8 hours** of occurrence; **Hospitalizations, amputations, loss of eye** – within **24 hours**. |  |

**Key dates**  
- **Fatality**: Report to OSHA within **8 hours**.  
- **Hospitalization, amputation, loss of eye**: Report to OSHA within **24 hours**.  
- **Form 300A** (annual summary) electronically filed by **March 2** of the following year, if the filing conditions above apply.  

**When you’re exempt**  
- If you employed ≤ 10 workers during the entire last calendar year **and** are not in a low‑hazard industry, you are *partially exempt* from recording requirements.  
- Some states have additional or different rules, so check your local OSHA‑approved State Plan.   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  

These records keep you compliant with OSHA’s 29 CFR 1904 *recordkeeping* requirements and allow you to demonstrate a proactive safety culture that protects employees and reduces costs.

runs.question: how do i register a trademark
runs.answer:
To register a trademark you need to:

1. Check that the mark isn’t already taken.  Search the state‑level trademark database and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) Trademark Electronic Search System (TESS) to make sure your desired name or logo hasn’t already been registered.  

2. Decide whether you want a state‑level mark or a federal mark.  A state registration gives you exclusive rights within that state, while a federal registration gives you nationwide protection and the right to use the “®” symbol.  

3. File the application.  
   * For a state registration, submit the application to the Secretary of State – for South Dakota you can contact the Secretary of State at (605) 773‑2797 or use their website at https://sdsos.gov/.  
   * For a federal registration, file with the USPTO (U.S. Patent and Trademark Office) at (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199, or use their website at www.uspto.gov.  

These steps give you exclusive rights to use the trademark in commerce.

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
**How long you must keep tax‑related records**

| Record type | Recommended retention period | Source |
|-------------|------------------------------|--------|
| **All other tax records** (e.g., receipts, invoices, bank statements, payroll documents) that support items on a tax return | Until the **period of limitation** expires for the year the return was filed (i.e., the time the IRS can assess additional tax or you can amend a return) | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Copies of filed tax returns** (the return itself and accompanying schedules) | Keep a copy forever, because it helps prepare future returns and prove what was filed | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Employment‑tax records** (time‑keeping, payroll reports, federal employment‑tax statements such as Forms 941, 944, 940) | For **at least 4 years** after the date the employment tax becomes due or the tax becomes paid, whichever is later | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Records relating to property (assets)** that you use for business or capital gains purposes | Keep until the period of limitation has expired for the year you **dispose of (sell, trade, otherwise dispose of)** the property | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Other records no longer needed for tax purposes** | Do **not discard** until you confirm that they are no longer required for other legal or business purposes (e.g., insurance, creditor claims) | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Period‑of‑limitations table (general**

| Situation | Limitation period | Source |
|-----------|-------------------|--------|
| Owe additional tax, or claim a refund, or amend a return | **3 years** | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |
| Fail to report income that should have been reported and is >25 % of gross income | **6 years** | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |
| File a fraudulent return | **No time limit** | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15) |

**Special note on refunds**

If you file a refund claim, you must do so **within 3 years from the date you filed the original return or 2 years from the date the tax was paid, whichever is later**. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=49)

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **They allow you to monitor the progress of your business.**  
   Good records let you see whether your business is improving, which products or services are selling well, and where you might need to change strategy. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
2. **They are required to prepare accurate financial statements.**  
   Income statements, balance sheets, cash‑flow statements, and payroll reports all come from the records you keep. These statements are useful for dealing with banks, creditors, and other stakeholders. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
3. **They support the income, expenses, and credits reported on your tax returns.**  
   The IRS can examine your returns at any time; if they ask you to explain an item, a complete set of records will speed the review and reduce the chance of penalties. The records must show how you arrived at the numbers on your return. “Your business records must…support the entries in your books and on your tax return.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
4. **They satisfy federal tax‑record‑keeping requirements and help you stay in compliance.**  
   The Internal Revenue Code requires you to keep records that may be needed for the administration of any provision of the code. “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
5. **They help you meet the IRS’s record‑retention limits.**  
   The period of limitations for an item of income or deduction (e.g., 3, 4, or 6 years) tells you how long you must keep the related documents. Employment‑tax records must be kept for 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
6. **They protect you in potential legal or audit situations.**  
   If the IRS conducts an audit or you face a legal claim, having the supporting documents (invoices, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, payroll records, etc.) allows you to demonstrate that your accounting was correct and that you complied with tax law. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

In short, keeping organized, accurate business records lets you manage your company effectively, file correct tax returns, prove compliance with the IRS, and protect your interests if a dispute arises.



**Sources:**

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
The segments explain how a business chooses an accounting method and when certain methods are required.  
In short, you pick either the **cash method** or the **accrual method** (or a combination that follows the rules).  

**Cash method** – Use this if you (1) are a sole‑prop or similar owner‑operator, (2) do *not* keep inventory, and (3) are a small‑business taxpayer. Income is reported when you receive it and expenses are deducted in the year you pay them.  
> "Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier to keep cash method records." [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

**Accrual method** – Required if you must keep inventory or if you have a larger business. Income is reported when earned, and expenses are deducted when incurred, whether or not you actually paid the money that year.  
> "Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the year you earn it … and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them … If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method …" [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

**Combination method** – Allowed only if it clearly shows income and follows the IRS rules (e.g., if inventory is required you must use accrual for purchases and sales; the rest can be cash).  
> "You can generally use any combination of cash, accrual, and special methods … However, if you use the cash method for figuring your income, you must use cash for reporting expenses …" [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

**When you need IRS approval** – If you change the method after your first return, you normally must file Form 3115 (or Form 1128 for tax‑year changes). Small businesses can sometimes get automatic approval.  
> "If you want to change the method ... you must ... generally get IRS approval before you can change to another method." [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

**So, what to do?**  
1. Determine if you have inventory.  
   *If no inventory → cash method is usually simplest.*  
2. If you *do* keep inventory or your business size requires it → accrual method.  
3. If you are a small business and you could count inventory as non‑incidental supplies, you can still use cash.  
   > "Certain small business taxpayers can use the cash method of accounting and can also account for inventoriable items as materials and supplies that are not incidental." [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

4. Once chosen, keep the same method for all tax years unless you file for a change with Form 3115 and receive IRS approval.  

**Summary**  
- **Cash**: no inventory, small business.  
- **Accrual**: inventory is required, or larger business.  
- **Combination**: only if it follows the IRS constraints above.  

Follow the citations above for the precise rules.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow a routine self‑inspection process as described in the handbook:

1. **Perform regular safety and health inspections**  
   *Schedule inspections that are frequent enough to capture changes in the workplace, such as new equipment, processes or materials.*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists**  
   *Select the checklists that apply to the areas most critical to your business. These checklists are based on OSHA standards and general safety principles; they provide a starting point for identifying hazards that you can then tailor to your specific work processes.*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Compile related information**  
   *Combine the completed checklists with injury/illness records, training records, and equipment maintenance logs. This helps you see where hazards remain after controls are applied and where new issues may arise.*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

4. **Review and update hazard controls**  
   *After identifying hazards, put in place controls and periodically re‑inspect to confirm the controls are still effective.*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

5. **Engage workers**  
   *Workers should be involved in the inspections, reporting potential hazards, and suggesting control improvements.*  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

6. **Document findings and actions**  
   *Keep records of inspections, the hazards found, the controls applied, and any follow‑up actions needed.*  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

By following these steps—conducting routine self‑inspections, using the handbook checklists, reviewing supporting records, and involving workers—you can systematically identify and manage hazards in your workplace.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
**Cash vs Accrual Accounting – What the IRS Says**

| Feature | Cash method | Accrual method |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| **When you report income** | In the year you **receive** the money (or it is constructively received) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) | In the year you **earn** it (when the right to the money is fixed, even if you don’t get paid yet) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |
| **When you report expenses** | In the year you **pay** the bill (or actually spend the cash) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) | In the year you **incur** the cost (when the liability is fixed and can be reasonably measured) – even if you don’t pay it until later [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |
| **Common example** | You get a $500 check on Dec 30, 2025 but can’t deposit it until Jan 3, 2026. You must include it in 2025 income because the check was constructively received in 2025, even though you didn’t have the cash until 2026. That’s the cash‑method rule for receipts [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) | You buy office supplies in December 2025, get the bill that month, but pay it in January 2026. Under accrual you can deduct the expense in 2025 because the liability was fixed and the cost can be determined – you matched the expense to the period when the supplies were used. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Inventory rule** | If you keep an inventory, you **must** use the accrual method for purchases and sales. Small business taxpayers may treat inventories as supplies and still use cash, but it is an exception. | Inventories are always valued on a yearly basis to compute cost of goods sold, so accrual is the default except for very small businesses. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Typical business size** | Many sole‑proprietors and small businesses without inventory use cash because it’s simpler and still allowed. | Businesses that produce, purchase, or sell merchandise usually need accrual because inventory tracks sales and costs. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5) |
| **Main difference in a nutshell** | Cash = “when you get the money” / “when you pay”  | Accrual = “when you earn the money” / “when you owe it” |

### Why the difference matters

1. **Timing of income & expenses** – The two methods can change the year a dollar is shown, which can affect your tax liability for that year.  
2. **Inventory & cost of goods sold** – Accrual provides a more accurate picture of profits for businesses that sell products, because it matches the cost of the goods sold with the revenue from those goods.  
3. **Simplicity vs precision** – Cash is easier to track for small operators who keep little or no inventory, while accrual gives a better picture for larger or inventory‑heavy businesses.

---

**Bottom line:**  
Under the *cash method* you count money only when you actually touch it; under the *accrual method* you count money when the earnings event occurs, whether or not payment has been made. The choice matters for when you report income, when you deduct expenses, and whether you must keep an inventory.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)
3. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

**What you can deduct**

| **Meals** | Actual cost (50 % deductible) or a standard meal allowance | 50 % of meals is usually deductible; you may use the museum's standard allowance instead of actual expenses | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) |
| **Baggage & shipping** (sending items between locations) | Actual cost | Must be ordinary and necessary for business | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35) |
| **Vehicle expenses** (operating, maintenance, insurance, parking, tolls) | Actual expenses **or** standard mileage rate (75 ¢/mile for 2025) | If you elect standard mileage, you can still deduct business‑related parking, tolls, and interest on a car loan | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Miscellaneous** (telephone, tips, cleaning) | Actual cost | Must be ordinary and necessary | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41) |

**Requirements for a deductible business trip**

1. **Away from your tax home**: Your duties must require you to be substantially farther from your regular workplace than a normal day’s work and you must need sleep or rest while away.  
2. **Ordinary and necessary**: The expense is common in your trade and helps you perform duties.  
3. **Keep records**: You must maintain receipts and log business purpose and miles.  

**Summary**

You can deduct travel expenses such as transport, lodging, meals (50 %) and vehicle costs (actual or standard mileage) when the trip meets the “away‑from‑home” test. Record each expense and keep documentation to back up the deduction.

runs.question: what goes in an executive summary
runs.answer:
The executive summary is a concise, one‑ to two‑paragraph snapshot that readers can skim for the key take‑away. It should:

* **State the business idea** – what you’re selling or providing and why it matters.  
* **Outline the financial need and funding use** – how much capital you’re seeking, what it will cover (start‑up costs, working capital, etc.), and how much you’ve already invested.  
* **Give a high‑level timeline of milestones** – when you expect to hit major goals such as product launch, first revenue, break‑even, etc.  
* **Be brief and to the point** – keep it short, clear, and compelling; write it last so you can reference the details in the rest of the plan.  

These elements should be captured in one or two paragraphs that give a quick but complete picture of your business and its growth prospects.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To describe your target market you should follow this outline:

1. **Identify the niche** – state who your best customers are.  
   - For a business market, break them down by industry, company size, location, or how they use the product.  
   - For a consumer (household) market, segment by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.  
   *Source: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)*  

2. **Give clear characteristics** – list the key traits that define each segment (e.g., “18‑35 year‑old urban professionals with disposable income”).  
   *Source: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)*  

3. **Estimate size and growth** – use population figures, industry reports, sales‑tax data, or other statistics to gauge the approximate size of each segment and its potential growth.  
   *Source: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)*  

4. **Show how much of the market you will capture** – state a realistic percentage of the total market you expect to serve.  
   *Source: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)*  

**Example**  
> “Our target market is urban, tech‑savvy professionals aged 25–40 who work in software development and are willing to pay a premium for eco‑friendly office supplies. According to the 2023 U.S. Census, there are roughly 5 million such professionals in the Seattle metro area, a market that is projected to grow 3 % annually.”

This structure gives a concise yet complete description of your target market.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes – because your shop is a **public accommodation** (a private business that sells goods or services to the public), the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requires you to remove physical barriers that are **readily achievable**.  
If you can adapt the shop so people who use wheelchairs can enter, move around, and access your services, you must do so. If a change is *not* readily achievable, the ADA allows you to provide an alternative method (e.g., phone orders, curb‑side pickup, or delivery) and to keep the business open to all customers, not just people with disabilities.  

**What the ADA requires for existing facilities**

- **Existing facilities are not exempt**; you cannot simply rely on a “grandfather” exception.  When a business serves the public, it must comply with the ADA’s accessibility obligations for existing facilities.  The goal is to remove barriers that are “readily achievable” (i.e., can be done without extreme difficulty or expense) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).

- **Barrier removal must be “readily achievable.”**  The definition depends on the size, type, and resources of your business.  Large businesses are expected to remove more barriers than small ones, and you can defer changes if you lack funds, but the obligation remains in the future as resources become available [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).

- **Key areas you must address first** –  
    * **Entrance** – a clear, accessible entrance (e.g., width ≥36 in., a ramp with slope ≤1:12, handrails, and a 30×48 in. clear floor space in front of any counter if the counter is not accessible) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
    * **Doors** – door hardware must be operable without grasping (lever handles, loop‑type handles).  Narrow revolving turnstiles must be replaced or bypassed [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13).  
    * **Aisles & maneuvering space** – 36‑in. wide aisles, at least 3 ft. by 3 ft. turning space, 30×48 in. clearance in front of counters, and 30 in. by 48 in. clearance at fixed seating or tables.  Shelving should be placed so they don’t block an accessible route [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17).  
    * **Market or service counters** – if a counter is higher than 36 in., provide a lowered section that is at least 36 in. long and no higher than 36 in. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
    * **Parking** – provide at least one accessible parking space (and, if total spaces ≤25, that space must also be van‑accessible) on level ground and an accessible route without steps or steep slopes [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9).

- **If a barrier cannot be removed readily**, you may provide an alternative method for access to goods and services (e.g., phone orders, curb‑side pickup, delivery, or a separate accessible area) and you must publicize that alternative [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11).

**Bottom line**

- **You do have to make your shop wheelchair accessible** if it can be done without a prohibitive cost or structural change.  
- If any element (door, aisle, counter, parking, entrance) is not readily achievable, you must still allow people with disabilities to access your services through alternative means and disclose those alternatives.

The ADA’s purpose is to ensure that everyone can use your shop in a way that is safe and convenient, so start by examining the specific accessibility elements listed above and plan the changes that are “readily achievable” for your business.

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
You are exempt from OSHA injury‑recordkeeping only if you meet the specific conditions listed in the regulations. According to the guidance you provided, employers are *partially exempt* from the requirement to keep OSHA Forms 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) and 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report) **if:**

1. **All employees** in the employer’s business were **ten or fewer** during each month of the entire last calendar year; or   
2. The employer operates in a **low‑hazard industry** as defined in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.  

Even if you qualify for this exemption, you must still **report** all work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye to OSHA within the required time periods [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: how long do i keep injury records
runs.answer:
You must retain OSHA injury records for at least five years.  
The OSHA Form 300 (log), Form 301 (incident report), and Form 300A (annual summary) must be kept at the worksite for a minimum of five years.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)
