runs.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
runs.answer:
To keep your employees safe **and** make sure the premises can be accessed by people with disabilities, you need a coordinated, written safety‐and‑access program that covers the following key areas:

| What you should do | Why it matters | Where it is stated in the handbook |
|---------------------|----------------|-------------------------------------|
| **1. Create a safety‑and‑health program** – management must lead it, involve workers, identify hazards, train and review it often. | A strong program reduces injuries, saves on insurance and legal costs, and builds a safer culture. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) describes the seven core elements; [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9) lists the required activities (reporting, inspections, training). |
| **2. Conduct regular workplace inspections** – check walkways, equipment, and the access route to see if they remain safe. | Spotting a new step, a wet floor, or a clogged door before a worker reaches it prevents accidents. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79) and [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78) give detailed clearance, cleaning, and repair requirements for walking‑working surfaces. |
| **3. Keep walkways clear and wide** – at least 36 in. for wheelchair maneuvering, 30 × 48 in. clear space in front of counters, and 3‑ft turning space for aisles. | Employees – especially those in wheelchairs – can move freely without tripping or slipping. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73) – aisles, shelves, and counters; [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) – in‑store aisles and turning spaces. |
| **4. Make entrances accessible** – a ramp (max 1:12 slope), side‑handrails (if rise > 6 in.), landing 18‑in. beyond the door, edge protection, and a clear route to the door. | People with mobility aids can enter without a step, and the route is usable in all weather. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10), [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) (ramp width ≥ 36 in., landing ≥ 18 in.), [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) (32‑in. opening if a turnstile is removed). |
| **5. Replace or add accessible gates next to turnstiles** – if a turnstile is required, the adjacent gate must be at least 32 in. wide. | Wheelchair users, walkers, or cane users cannot push through narrow turnstiles. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) details turning‑gate width requirements. |
| **6. Install signage** that points to the accessible entrance when a building has a non‑accessible primary door. | People who can’t use the primary entrance immediately see where to go. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) – “a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance”. |
| **7. Provide accessible parking** – sign with the international symbol, 5‑ft aisle (or 8‑ft for vans), and a level access path to the building entrance. | Employees and customers arriving by car can reach the building without stairs or steps. | [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) (parking spaces, aisle width), [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) (signage, routing). |
| **8. Install and maintain safe exit routes** – at least two exits from elevated areas, exit signs 6 in. high, emergency lighting, and a clear chain of command for evacuations. | In a fire or other emergency, everyone can evacuate quickly and safely. | [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26) (evacuation plan, exit signage), [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28) (evidence of exit signs), [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54) (exits listed). |
| **9. Protect workers from falling hazards** – guardrails, safety nets, headroom, and PPE for any elevated work. | Falls are among the most common serious injuries in small businesses. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73) (guardrails, safety nets, PPE). |
| **10. Keep machinery and equipment safe** – clean, maintenance, lockout, manual controls, emergency stop buttons. | Prevents accidental starts, burns or other equipment‑related injuries. | [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54) (equipment safety checklist). |
| **11. Provide training on workplace violence** – a written program with policies, training, patrol, or alarm systems. | Reduces the risk of assaults and improves how employees respond to violent incidents. | [[15]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=85) (workplace violence checklist). |
| **12. Remove architectural barriers** – widening doorways to ≥ 36 in. clear, installing lever handles, widening aisles, and keeping “platforms” to ≥ 36 in. | Enables employees (and customers) with a variety of mobility limitations to move around safely. | [[16]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) (door and hardware), [[17]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7) (barrier removal checklist). |

**Practical steps you can start with immediately**

1. **Audit your premises** using the inspection checklists in [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79) and [Segment

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
**How to write a business plan**

1. **Cover page** – put the company name, address, phone number, owners’ contact info, logo, and date of the plan.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

2. **Table of contents** – optional, but useful for long plans.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

3. **Executive summary** – a concise one‑to‑two‑paragraph overview that tells the reader what the business is, how much money you need, where the money will go, and a short schedule of goals.  Draft this last.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

4. **Business description** – describe the product/service, how it gives you a sustainable competitive advantage, the regulations that apply, the facilities and equipment you need, and the overall industry outlook.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

5. **Management plan** – outline the organizational structure, list owners and their ownership percentages, and describe key managers’ responsibilities, qualifications and day‑to‑day duties.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

6. **Market analysis** – estimate the total market, focus on your target market, analyze competition, and explain how you will make and promote your product/service.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

7. **Financial (money) section** – present the startup cost summary, a 3‑year income projection, a statement of cash flow, a balance sheet, and a break‑even analysis.  Include supporting documents such as your “Sources and Uses” sheet and notes on critical assumptions.  The SBDC can help you prepare these four key documents.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  

8. **Exhibits** – attach resumes, purchase agreements, bids, contracts, floor plans, or any other document that substantiates what is written in the plan.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  

9. **Review and refine** – ask a mentor, accountant, or SCORE/SBDC advisor to review the plan and provide feedback before finalizing.  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  


**Setting up accounting**

1. **Choose a legal and tax structure** – decide on sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, or LLC, obtain an EIN if you’ll have employees, and file the appropriate formation documents (articles of incorporation, name registration, etc.).  
   [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  

2. **Open a dedicated business checking account** – keep it separate from personal funds, use it for all deposits and withdrawals, and keep the account address in your business records.  
   [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

3. **Use a business checkbook / register** – record each expense the day it occurs, note the source of each receipt, and write checks only for documented expenditures.  Avoid paying cash unless you keep a proper receipt and note the reason.  
   [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

4. **Decide on an accounting method**  
   * **Cash method** – record income when received and expenses when paid (often used if you have no inventory).  
   * **Accrual method** – record income when earned and expenses when incurred (required if you keep inventory or have significant accounts receivable).  
   * You may need IRS approval to change methods.  
   [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

5. **Pick a bookkeeping system**  
   * **Single‑entry** – simple, tracks income and expenses with daily and monthly cash receipt



**Sources:**

to the basis of depreciable property. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40) | | **Maintenance & repair of business premises** | Repair invoices, contractor bills. | Ordinary and necessary repairs to a business location are deductible. | personal records** – This is crucial for items that you use for both, like a car or credit card. * Keep a dedicated business checkbook or credit card, and a separate set of personal payment records. * For mixed‑use items, keep a log that shows the business portion. * Compare the business portion to the total cost to calculate the deductible percentage. * runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
Yes, you need an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if your business

* hires one or more employees, or  
* must file pension or excise‑tax returns, or  
* chooses to use an EIN instead of its owner’s Social‑Security number for tax‑identification purposes.  

These requirements are stated in the IRS publication excerpts: *“If you must have an EIN, include it along with your SSN on your Schedule C (Form 1040) as instructed.”* and *“You must also have an EIN to use as a TIN if you do either of the following… Pay wages to one or more employees. File pension or excise tax returns.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)【5】.  
Even when you are a sole proprietor with no employees, you may still obtain an EIN; the publication notes: *“If your business will hire employees or pay Federal Excise Tax, a Federal Employer’s Identification Number (EIN) must be obtained.”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)【18】.  

**What accounting method do you choose?**  
An EIN does not dictate a particular accounting method.  When you file your first income‑tax return, you must choose an accounting method—**cash** or **accrual** (or a special/combination method if required).  

* Cash method: report income in the year it is received and match expenses to the year they are paid.  
* Accrual method: report income in the year it is earned and match expenses to the year they are incurred, whether or not you pay them then.  

If you have inventory that must be accounted for, the default rule is to use an accrual method for purchases and sales; a small‑business taxpayer may use a cash method for inventory that is treated as “non‑incidental material or supplies.”  (See *“If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for purchases and sales.”* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) and *“If you are a small business taxpayer, you can choose not to keep an inventory, but you must still use a method of accounting for inventory that clearly reflects income.”* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)​).

Thus, you can apply for an EIN at any time that meets the above criteria, and you choose your accounting method independently—most small businesses with no inventory use the cash method, while businesses that maintain inventory typically use the accrual method unless the small‑business exception applies.

runs.question: do i need workers comp insurance and can i deduct it
runs.answer:
**Do you need workers’ compensation insurance?**  
Yes.  Workers’ compensation insurance is required by state law for any employee that can be injured on the job, and the law requires you to carry it whenever you have employees.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37)  

**Can you deduct the premiums you pay?**  
Yes.  Premiums for workers’ compensation insurance are deductible as a business expense on Schedule C (Form 1040).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37)  

(If you’re unsure whether your particular state requires it, the state Department of Labor website is a reliable reference.)

runs.question: what do i file for my employees and what state taxes do i owe for them
runs.answer:
**Federal forms you must file for each employee**

| What you owe | What to file | When it’s due (for a calendar‑year business) | Source |
|--------------|--------------|---------------------------------------------|--------|
| Federal income‑tax withholding, Social Security and Medicare taxes (the employer’s share) | **Form 941** (Employer’s QUARTERLY Federal Tax Return) *or* **Form 944** (Employer’s ANNUAL Federal Tax Return) if you qualify | 4th month **April 30**, 6th month **July 31**, 9th month **October 31**, 1st month after year **January 31** (or the next business day if those dates fall on a weekend) | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| Annual summary of wages, tips, and all employer tax payments | **Form W‑3**, Summary of W‑2s | January 31 (or the next business day) | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| Wages, tips, and employer tax information to give each employee | **Form W‑2**, Wage and Tax Statement | Every employee receives a copy by January 31 (or next business day) | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7) |
| Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) tax | **Form 940**, Employer’s Annual Federal Unemployment (FUTA) Tax Return | January 31 each year (or the next business day if that falls on a weekend) | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7) |

If you hire new employees, you also need to get them to complete **Form I‑9** (Employment Eligibility Verification) and **Form W‑4** (Employee’s Withholding Certificate) before you start paying wages. Those forms are not filed with the IRS but are required on file at your business.  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=7)

---

**State‑level obligations**

* **State unemployment insurance tax**  
  • As an employer, you must make **quarterly payments to the state’s unemployment insurance fund**.  
  • For example, in South Dakota you must file contributions with the Department of Labor, Division of Unemployment Insurance, and remit the tax each quarter.  
  • This is a separate state tax from the federal FUTA and is due every quarter.  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9)

* **State income‑tax withholding**  
  • If your state has an income‑tax withholding requirement for employees, you must withhold the employee’s state tax from paychecks and remit it to the state tax authority.  
  • The specific withholding form and due dates vary by state; consult your state’s department of revenue for details.  
  (The segments above do not list a particular state form, but the requirement is a standard part of state tax law.)  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=9) (general reference to state withholding obligations)

If you have other state‑specific taxes (e.g., state excise, sales/usage, meal and lodging taxes, or local taxes), you must file the corresponding state forms and remit those taxes as required. The above list covers the most common payroll‑related state obligations.

runs.question: what if a customer cannot get through my front door and what if someone is hurt on site
runs.answer:
**If a customer cannot get through your front‑door entrance**

1. **Give them an alternative accessible entrance** – if the main door is not usable, you must provide another publicly‑accessible entrance that is compliant with the ADA.  
   *The ADA requires that: “When one entrance is not accessible and another entrance is accessible, a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance.  The alternative entrance must be open during store hours.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

2. **Clear signage and lighting** – place a sign that clearly points from the main entrance to the alternative entrance.  The sign should be mounted at an accessible height (generally ≤ 48 in. above the ground).  If a security gate keeps the alternative door locked, install a buzzer or call‑bell that is positioned on an accessible route and is no more than 48 in. tall.  The “buzzer or call bell” must be placed so a wheelchair user can reach it. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

3. **Keep the alternative door unlocked during business hours** – the door that serves as the secondary entrance must remain unlocked.  If the door can’t be kept unlocked for security reasons, provide a door‑open system (unlocked handle, call box, etc.) that is accessible. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

4. **If the main entry has a turnstile** – remove the turnstile or replace it with an accessible gate.  The opening must be at least 32 in. wide (or as wide as practicable) and must be left open during hours. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)  

5. **Re‑evaluate the main entrance** – where possible, modify the existing door: add a ramp, eliminate a single step, or reinstall a lever handle so that the primary door itself becomes accessible.  These modifications are lower‑cost ways to avoid reliance on a secondary entrance. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

---

**If someone is hurt on the site**

1. **First‑aid readiness** – the site must have a fully supplied first‑aid kit that is easy to reach from each area and is inspected and replenished regularly.  At least one worker on each shift must be trained and qualified to render first aid.  If a medical facility is not nearby, you must have first‑aid trained staff and the required protective gear. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=62)  

2. **Medical personnel** – if staff are expected to respond to medical emergencies, they should receive first‑aid training, hepatitis B vaccination, and be trained on universal precautions. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=62)  

3. **Record‑keeping** – record all occupational injuries (except trivial first‑aid‑only cases) on OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses).  For each recordable incident, file Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report).  At year‑end, produce Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses).  Employers with 250+ workers, or 20–249 in high‑hazard industries, must file Form 300A electronically by **March 2** of the following year. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  

4. **Reporting serious incidents** – any fatality, in‑patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye must be reported to OSHA immediately.  

5. **Emergency planning** – maintain a written workplace‑violence and emergency plan that includes clear procedures for calling security or police, and drill the staff on what to do if an injury occurs.  OSHA recommends that all employees be trained on the emergency program. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=85)  

By following the above steps you will ensure that customers who cannot use the front door are still able to enter and that any on‑site injuries are handled promptly, safely, and in compliance with OSHA record‑keeping requirements.



**Sources:**

runs.question: how much cash before i have to report it and do i need a licence to serve food
runs.answer:
You must report large cash takings and you need a food‑service license if you intend to prepare and serve food.

**Cash reporting**

* If you receive **more than $10,000 in cash in a single transaction, or in two or more related business transactions,** you are required to file **Form 8300, “Report of Cash Payments Over $10,000 Received in a Trade or Business.”**  
  *Cash includes U.S. and foreign coin and currency, as well as cashier’s checks, traveler’s checks and money orders. Personal checks are not counted.*  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  

**License to serve food**

* Any business that prepares and serves food must first have its premises inspected by the local **Health Department**. Only after that inspection can a **food license** (or a lodging license, if the business also provides lodging) be issued.  
* If you plan to sell alcohol, you will need separate liquor, beer or wine licenses from your local city or county government.  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=8)  

So: report cash when you cross the $10,000 threshold with Form 8300, and obtain a health‑department food license (and possibly an alcohol license) before serving food.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 12)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)
2. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 8)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=8)

runs.question: why should i bother with a safety program and what records do i need to keep
runs.answer:
A safety program is a worthwhile investment because it protects workers, keeps the business compliant, and saves money.  In the handbook it is described as a way to “prevent workplace injuries and illnesses, improve compliance with laws and regulations, reduce costs (including significant reductions in workers’‑compensation premiums), engage workers, enhance social‑responsibility goals, and increase productivity and overall business operations” – all of which are highlighted as benefits of a safety and health program [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6).

In addition, a safety program must be documented and maintained.  The handbook specifies the records you must keep and how long to keep them:

* **Injury and illness records** – Every recordable injury or illness (except minor first‑aid cases) is entered on OSHA Form 300, and a detailed Incident Report is filed on OSHA Form 301.  These records must be kept at the worksite for at least five years [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
* **Summary records** – At the end of each calendar year you must prepare an annual summary on OSHA Form 300A.  For businesses that need to report (see below) the summary must be electronically submitted to OSHA by **March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered** [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
* **Medical and exposure records** – Worker medical records and exposure records must be retained for the period required for each specific type of record, and must be accessible to workers as required by OSHA [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
* **Training records** – Records of safety and health training (including worker‑specific training) must be kept and must be easily reviewable by workers [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
* **Fatalities and severe injuries** – All work‑related fatalities must be reported to OSHA within **8 hours**, and all hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye must be reported within **24 hours** [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  

Reporting requirements vary by business size and industry:

* If your establishment has **100 or more workers** in a high‑hazard industry, you must electronically submit Form 300A by March 2 [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
* If you have **250 or more workers** (or 20–249 workers in certain high‑rate industries) you are also required to submit Form 300A by March 2 [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).  
* Employers with **10 or fewer workers** (or in certain low‑hazard industries) are partially exempt from these record‑keeping rules [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).  

Keeping these records demonstrates compliance, supports investigation of incidents, and helps you track safety performance.  The handbook makes clear that a written safety program, regular self‑inspections, and proper record‑keeping together create a culture of safety that protects workers and the business alike [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7).



**Sources:**

runs.question: how do i register a trademark
runs.answer:
You can register a trademark either at the state level or at the federal level.  
At the state level you file through your state’s Secretary of State office; at the federal level you file through the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).

**State‑level registration**  
- Contact the South Dakota Secretary of State (depending on your state the contact will be similar).  
  Phone: (605) 773‑2797  
  Website: https://sdsos.gov/  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

**Federal‑level registration**  
- File with the USPTO.  
  Phone: (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199  
  Website: www.uspto.gov  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

Before filing, you should search trademark databases to make sure the name or mark has not already been registered, which will also help you determine whether a state or federal application is appropriate. The documents only provide contact information and the basic fact that registration can be done at either level; no specific deadlines or step‑by‑step instructions are given in the provided segments.
